entry.title: Bias-Aware Inference in Regularized Regression Models

link.title: Bias-Aware Inference in Regularized Regression Models

entry.content: We consider inference on a scalar regression coefficient under a constraint on the magnitude of the control coefficients. A class of estimators based on a regularized propensity score regression is shown to exactly solve a tradeoff between worst-case bias and variance. We derive confidence intervals (CIs) based on these estimators that are bias-aware: they account for the possible bias of the estimator. Under homoskedastic Gaussian errors, these estimators and CIs are near-optimal in finite samples for mean squared error and CI length. We also provide conditions for asymptotic validity of the CIs with an unknown and possibly heteroskedastic error distribution, and derive novel optimal rates of convergence under high-dimensional asymptotics that allow the number of regressors to increase more quickly than the number of observations. Extensive simulations and two empirical applications illustrate the performance of our methods.

entry.title: Population Neuroscience 3.0: Bridging large-N and small-N paradigms in brain-wide association studies

link.title: Population Neuroscience 3.0: Bridging large-N and small-N paradigms in brain-wide association studies

entry.content: Brain-wide association studies (BWAS) leveraging large datasets, have led to divergent and sometimes opposing views on research practices and priorities. The debates span multiple dimensions, including large-N vs.\ small-N sampling, cross-sectional vs.\ longitudinal, observational vs.\ interventional/causal, population generalizability vs.\ individual specificity, data-driven vs.\ hypothesis-driven, prediction-oriented vs.\ explanation-oriented, and molecular/cellular vs.\ systems-level. Taken together, these tensions are not only about methodology, but also about how large-N population studies and small-N, mechanism-focused studies should relate to one another. Shifts along these axes have sharpened disagreements and added to fragmentation in an already heterogeneous field of cognitive neuroscience. Here, we sketch an integrative response grounded in population neuroscience, organized around a closed-loop design--analysis--interpretation'' research cycle that aims to build consensus while bridging these divides. Our central claim is that population neuroscience offers a distinctive population-level vantage point for identifying general patterns, characterizing inter-individual variabilities, and benchmarking intra-individual changes, thereby providing reference frameworks through which small-N, mechanism-focused studies can co-evolve with large-N population studies. Population neuroscience is not simply about providing larger N for BWAS; more fundamentally, it is about accumulating cross-scale priors and shared infrastructures for design, analysis, and interpretation across human neuroscience studies. In this sense, we outline athird-generation’’ agenda for population neuroscience that shifts emphasis from amassing isolated associations to building reference frameworks for cumulative mechanistic and translational research.

entry.title: A robust multivariate, non-parametric outlier identification method for scrubbing in fMRI

link.title: A robust multivariate, non-parametric outlier identification method for scrubbing in fMRI

entry.content: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data contain high levels of noise and artifacts. To avoid contamination of downstream analyses, fMRI-based studies must identify and remove these noise sources prior to statistical analysis. One common approach is the “scrubbing” of fMRI volumes that are thought to contain high levels of noise. However, existing scrubbing techniques are based on ad hoc measures of signal change. We consider scrubbing via outlier detection, where volumes containing artifacts are considered multidimensional outliers. Robust multivariate outlier detection methods are proposed using robust distances (RDs), which are related to the Mahalanobis distance. These RDs have a known distribution when the data are i.i.d. normal, and that distribution can be used to determine a threshold for outliers where fMRI data violate these assumptions. Here, we develop a robust multivariate outlier detection method that is applicable to non-normal data. The objective is to obtain threshold values to flag outlying volumes based on their RDs. We propose two threshold candidates that embark on the same two steps, but the choice of which depends on a researcher’s purpose. Our main steps are dimension reduction and selection, robust univariate outlier imputation to get rid of the effect of outliers on the distribution, and estimating an outlier threshold based on the upper quantile of the RD distribution without outliers. The first threshold candidate is an upper quantile of the empirical distribution of RDs obtained from the imputed data. The second threshold candidate calculates the upper quantile of the RD distribution that a nonparametric bootstrap uses to account for uncertainty in the empirical quantile. We compare our proposed fMRI scrubbing method to motion scrubbing, data-driven scrubbing, and restrictive parametric multivariate outlier detection methods.

entry.title: Optimized Conformal Selection: Powerful Selective Inference After Data-Dependent Score Construction

link.title: Optimized Conformal Selection: Powerful Selective Inference After Data-Dependent Score Construction

entry.content: We study data-driven score construction in conformal selection, which uses conformal p-values and multiple testing to select “interesting” instances with large unobserved labels from a pool of unlabeled data, while controlling the FDR in finite sample. While existing solutions require the score function to be constructed independent of the calibration and test data, it is desirable to select or construct powerful conformity score in a data-driven manner and to leverage all labeled data for score training when presented with many score choices and limited labeled data. We propose Optimized Conformal Selection (OptCS), a general framework that allows valid multiple testing after flexible data-driven score construction. We introduce general conditions under which OptCS constructs valid conformal p-values despite substantial data reuse and handles complex p-value dependencies to maintain finite-sample FDR control. We instantiate this general recipe to propose three FDR-controlling procedures, each optimizing the models differently: (i) selecting a powerful score function among multiple candidates, (ii) training the score with all labeled data without sample splitting, and (iii) combining full-sample training and model selection. We demonstrate the efficacy of our methods via simulation studies and real applications in drug discovery and large language models.

entry.title: Network Cross-Validation and Model Selection via Subsampling

link.title: Network Cross-Validation and Model Selection via Subsampling

entry.content: Complex and larger networks are becoming increasingly prevalent in scientific applications in various domains. Although a number of models and methods exist for such networks, cross-validation on networks remains challenging due to the unique structure of network data. In this paper, we propose a general cross-validation procedure called NETCROP (NETwork CRoss-Validation using Overlapping Partitions). The key idea is to divide the original network into multiple subnetworks with a shared overlap part, producing training sets consisting of the subnetworks and a test set with the node pairs between the subnetworks. This train-test split provides the basis for a network cross-validation procedure that can be applied on a wide range of model selection and parameter tuning problems for networks. The method is computationally efficient for large networks as it uses smaller subnetworks for the training step. We provide methodological details and theoretical guarantees for several model selection and parameter tuning tasks using NETCROP. Numerical results demonstrate that NETCROP performs accurate cross-validation on a diverse set of network model selection and parameter tuning problems. The results also indicate that NETCROP is computationally much faster while being often more accurate than the existing methods for network cross-validation.

entry.title: The dynamic generalized covariance measure for conditional independence testing with nonstationary time series

link.title: The dynamic generalized covariance measure for conditional independence testing with nonstationary time series

entry.content: Identifying relationships among stochastic processes is a core objective in many fields, such as economics. While the standard toolkit for multivariate time series analysis has many advantages, it can be difficult to capture nonlinear dynamics using linear vector autoregressive models. This difficulty has motivated the development of methods for causal discovery and variable selection for nonlinear time series, which routinely employ tests for conditional independence. In this paper, we introduce the first framework for conditional independence testing that works with a single realization of a nonstationary nonlinear process. The proposed test is designed to have power against alternatives in which the expected conditional covariance is non-zero for at least some times. We also discuss an approach for gaining power against a broader range of alternatives. The key technical ingredients of our framework are time-varying nonlinear regression, estimation of local long-run covariance matrices of products of error processes, and a distribution-uniform strong Gaussian approximation.

entry.title: Can synthetic data reproduce real-world findings in epidemiology? A replication study using adversarial random forests

link.title: Can synthetic data reproduce real-world findings in epidemiology? A replication study using adversarial random forests

entry.content: Synthetic data hold substantial potential to address practical challenges in epidemiology due to restricted data access and privacy concerns. However, many current methods suffer from limited quality, high computational demands, and complexity for non-experts. Furthermore, common evaluation strategies for synthetic data often fail to directly reflect statistical utility and measure privacy risks sufficiently. Against this background, a critical underexplored question is whether synthetic data can reliably reproduce key findings from epidemiological research while preserving privacy. We propose adversarial random forests (ARF) as an efficient and convenient method for synthesizing tabular epidemiological data. To evaluate its performance, we replicated statistical analyses from six epidemiological publications covering blood pressure, anthropometry, myocardial infarction, accelerometry, loneliness, and diabetes, from the German National Cohort (NAKO Gesundheitsstudie), the Bremen STEMI Registry U45 Study, and the Guelph Family Health Study. We further assessed how dataset dimensionality and variable complexity affect the quality of synthetic data, and contextualized ARF’s performance by comparison with commonly used tabular data synthesizers in terms of utility, privacy, generalization, and runtime. Across all replicated studies, results on ARF-generated synthetic data consistently aligned with original findings. Even for datasets with relatively low sample size-to-dimensionality ratios, replication outcomes closely matched the original results across descriptive and inferential analyses. Reduced dimensionality and variable complexity further enhanced synthesis quality. ARF demonstrated favourable performance regarding utility, privacy preservation, and generalization relative to other synthesizers and superior computational efficiency.

entry.title: A Computable Measure of Suboptimality for Entropy-Regularised Variational Objectives

link.title: A Computable Measure of Suboptimality for Entropy-Regularised Variational Objectives

entry.content: Several methods in statistics and machine learning target a probability distribution for which an entropy-regularised variational objective is minimised. This increased flexibility introduces a computational challenge, as one loses access to an explicit unnormalised density for the target. To mitigate this difficulty, we introduce a novel measure of suboptimality called ‘gradient discrepancy’, and in particular a kernel gradient discrepancy (KGD) that can be explicitly computed. In the Bayesian statistics context, KGD coincides with the kernel Stein discrepancy (KSD), and we obtain a novel characterisation of KSD as measuring the size of a variational gradient. Outside this familiar setting, KGD enables novel sampling algorithms to be developed and compared, even when unnormalised densities cannot be obtained. To illustrate this point several novel algorithms are proposed and studied, including a natural generalisation of Stein variational gradient descent, with applications to mean-field neural networks and predictively oriented posteriors presented. On the theoretical side, our principal contribution is to establish sufficient conditions for desirable properties of KGD, such as continuity and convergence control.

entry.title: Correlation of divergency: c_delta. Being different in a similar way or not

link.title: Correlation of divergency: c_delta. Being different in a similar way or not

entry.content: Matched sets may have unlike mean scores and spreads yet share the same way in which some scores stand apart. Mean gaps and raw-score correlations do not answer this question. Correlation of divergency, c_delta, is put forward to fill that gap. For every score in each of two equally sized, matched sets, it finds how far that score lies from every other score in its own set. It then draws these gaps into one divergence score through a power mean. The Pearson correlation between the two lists of divergence scores is c_delta, which lies between -1 and 1. A high positive value means that the same people or things stand out in both sets, no matter which way their raw scores point. A negative value means that a score far from the rest in one set tends to be matched with a score near the rest in the other, whilst a value near zero shows little linear link. As c_delta stems from within-set gaps, it is unchanged by shifts in overall level or units. It can show whether the same people feel sharply shut out in matched neighbourhood sets, whether the same bacterial strains grow oddly under two drugs, or whether the same proteins stand out in two drug-binding fingerprints. It should sit alongside means and raw-score correlations rather than take their place: c_delta does not show whether an outlier is high or low, nor why it arose. The power p sets the weight given to wide gaps. With p=1 it uses Gini distance, and with p=2 root-mean-square distance. Higher p gives more weight to the furthest gaps but cuts Kish’s effective sample size. The raw scores and the choice of p must therefore be read with care.

entry.title: Detecting Model Misspecification in Bayesian Inverse Problems via Variational Gradient Descent

link.title: Detecting Model Misspecification in Bayesian Inverse Problems via Variational Gradient Descent

entry.content: Bayesian inference is optimal when the statistical model is well-specified, while outside this setting Bayesian inference can catastrophically fail; accordingly a wealth of post-Bayesian methodologies have been proposed. Predictively oriented (PrO) approaches lift the statistical model $P_\theta$ to an (infinite) mixture model $\int P_\theta \; \mathrm{d}Q(\theta)$ and fit this predictive distribution via minimising an entropy-regularised objective functional. In the well-specified setting one expects the mixing distribution $Q$ to concentrate around the true data-generating parameter in the large data limit, while such singular concentration will typically not be observed if the model is misspecified. Our contribution is to demonstrate that one can empirically detect model misspecification by comparing the standard Bayesian posterior to the PrO `posterior’ $Q$, providing a novel and widely-applicable diagnostic tool for the standard Bayesian workflow. To operationalise this, we present an efficient numerical algorithm based on variational gradient descent. A simulation study, and a more detailed case study involving a Bayesian inverse problem in seismology, confirm that model misspecification can be automatically detected using this framework.

entry.title: Covariate-assisted graph matching

link.title: Covariate-assisted graph matching

entry.content: Data integration often requires aligning datasets without unique identifiers; for network data this is commonly addressed through graph matching. Despite the widespread availability of node and edge covariates in many applications, most existing methods rely solely on the structural similarity between the two graphs, limiting their flexibility and robustness to non-identifiable matches and structural noise. In this article, we study the seeded graph matching problem, where a partial alignment for a set of nodes (seeds) is known, in the presence of informative node and edge covariates. We propose two covariate-assisted methods: a global approach based on a quadratic assignment problem (QAP), and a scalable local approach that leverages the neighborhood of the seeds. Both methods are based on a flexible conditional modeling framework that enables covariate integration using predictive models ranging from generalized linear models to machine learning methods. We provide estimation error rates for the generalized linear model, and sufficient conditions for exact recovery of the true correspondences via the QAP. We further specialize these results to Erd\H{o}s-R'enyi model with covariates. The effectiveness in achieving improved performance by leveraging additional covariates is demonstrated through simulations and in an application to matching the statistics academic genealogy and the collaboration networks.

entry.title: Simulation of warping processes with applications to temperature data

link.title: Simulation of warping processes with applications to temperature data

entry.content: Curve registration plays a major role in functional data analysis by separating amplitude and phase variation through warping functions and the accurate simulation of warping processes is essential for developing statistical methods that properly account for phase variability in functional data. In this paper, we focus on the simulation of continuous warping processes with a prescribed expectation and a controllable variance. We study and compare three procedures, including two existing methods and a new algorithm based on randomized empirical cumulative distribution functions. For each approach, we provide an operational description and establish theoretical results for the first two moments of the simulated processes. A numerical study illustrates the theoretical findings and highlights the respective merits of the three methods. Finally, we present an application to the analysis of hourly temperature data spatially averaged over Canada, based on simulated realizations from a warping process estimated using spatially averaged temperature quantile functions.

entry.title: Best Feasible Conditional Critical Values for a More Powerful Subvector Anderson-Rubin Test

link.title: Best Feasible Conditional Critical Values for a More Powerful Subvector Anderson-Rubin Test

entry.content: For subvector inference in the linear instrumental variables model under homoskedasticity but allowing for weak instruments, Guggenberger, Kleibergen and Mavroeidis (2019) (GKM) propose a conditional subvector Anderson and Rubin (1949) (AR) test that uses data-dependent critical values that adapt to the strength of the parameters not under test. This test has correct size and strictly higher power than the test that uses standard asymptotic chi-square critical values. The subvector AR test is the minimum eigenvalue of a data-dependent matrix. The GKM critical value function conditions on the largest eigenvalue of this matrix. Instead, this paper considers a data-dependent critical value function that conditions on the second-smallest eigenvalue, as this eigenvalue is the appropriate indicator of weak identification. We find that the data-dependent critical value function of GKM also applies to this conditioning and show that this test has correct size and power strictly higher than the GKM test when the number of parameters not under test is larger than one. This is the best feasible test, where we consider feasible to be within the class of conditioning on a single eigenvalue. Our proposed procedure further applies to the subvector AR test statistic that is robust to an approximate Kronecker product structure of conditional heteroskedasticity as proposed by Guggenberger, Kleibergen and Mavroeidis (2024), carrying over its power advantage to this setting as well.

entry.title: Phase Transitions in Collective Damage of Civil Structures under Natural Hazards

link.title: Phase Transitions in Collective Damage of Civil Structures under Natural Hazards

entry.content: The fate of cities under natural hazards depends not only on hazard intensity but also on the coupling of structural damage, a collective process that remains poorly understood. Here we show that urban structural damage exhibits phase-transition phenomena. As hazard intensity increases, the system can shift abruptly from a largely safe to a largely damaged state, analogous to a discontinuous phase transition in statistical physics. Higher diversity in the building portfolio smooths this transition, but multiscale damage clustering traps the system in a highly volatile regime that suppresses the emergence of predictable Gaussian statistics. The observed phenomenological patterns are interpreted through an effective random-field Ising model, with its key parameters translated into tangible engineering variables such as hazard demand, structural diversity, and modeling uncertainty. These insights establish a phase-aware description of collective damage, revealing that common engineering simplifications can distort the inherent phase of real urban portfolios. Critically, such phase distortions can substantially bias hazard loss estimates, producing relative errors of up to 50% in exceedance probabilities under moderate earthquakes—equivalent to a several-fold gap in anticipated repair costs. The phase-aware description turns the collective behavior of civil infrastructure damage into actionable diagnostics for urban risk assessment and planning.

entry.title: Forge: An Agentic System for ERGM Specification and Interpretation in Social Networks

link.title: Forge: An Agentic System for ERGM Specification and Interpretation in Social Networks

entry.content: Exponential Random Graph Models (ERGMs) provide a statistical framework for testing hypotheses about how ties form using network structure and node attributes. We present Forge (Formation-Oriented Reasoning with Guarded ERGMs), an agentic system that performs this process using a language model and external statistical tools. Given an observed network and a domain description, Forge proposes hypotheses about tie formation, translates them into candidate ERGM specifications, evaluates them statistically, refines the best candidate using goodness-of-fit feedback, and returns a human-readable interpretation of the final model. On 16 benchmark networks, Forge improves on the best baseline on 13 networks and matches it on the other three, with a median 24.8% improvement in goodness of fit. On 60 controlled networks with known generating specifications, Forge achieves exact specification recovery in 78.3% of cases and attains 90.8% term-level F1. These results show that Forge can reduce the manual trial-and-error involved in ERGM specification while making the process more reproducible and keeping model selection grounded in statistical evidence.

entry.title: A note on conditional densities, Bayes’ rule, and recent criticisms of Bayesian inference

link.title: A note on conditional densities, Bayes’ rule, and recent criticisms of Bayesian inference

entry.content: When performing Bayesian inference, we frequently need to work with conditional probability densities. For example, the posterior function is the conditional density of the parameters given the data. Some might worry that conditional densities are ill-defined, considering that for a continuous random variable $Y$, the event ${Y=y}$ has probability zero, meaning the formula $\mathbb{P}(A B)=\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)/\mathbb{P}(B)$ is inapplicable. In reality, when we work with conditional densities, we never condition directly on the zero-probability event ${Y=y}$; rather, we first condition on the random variable $Y$, and then we may plug in an observed value $y$. The first purpose of our article is to provide an exposition on conditional densities that elaborates on this point. While we have aimed to make this explanation accessible, we follow it with a roadmap of the measure theory needed to make it rigorous. A recent preprint (arXiv:2411.13570) has expressed the concern that probability densities are ill-defined and that as a result Bayes’ theorem cannot be used, and they provide examples that allegedly demonstrate inconsistencies in the Bayesian framework. The second purpose of our article is to investigate their claims. We contend that the examples given in their work do not demonstrate any inconsistencies; we find that there are mathematical errors and that they deviate significantly from the Bayesian framework.

entry.title: Bayesian Semiparametric Multivariate Density Regression with Coordinate-Wise Predictor Selection

link.title: Bayesian Semiparametric Multivariate Density Regression with Coordinate-Wise Predictor Selection

entry.content: We propose a flexible Bayesian approach for estimating the joint density of a multivariate random variable of interest in the presence of categorical covariates. Leveraging a Gaussian copula framework, our method captures the dependence structure across different coordinates of the multivariate response. The conditional (on covariates) marginal (across outcomes) distributions are modeled as flexible mixtures with shared atoms across coordinates. The mixture weights are allowed to vary with covariates through a novel Tucker tensor factorization-based structure which enables the identification of coordinate-specific subsets of influential covariates. In particular, we replace the traditional mode matrices with coordinate-specific random partition models on the covariate levels, offering a flexible mechanism to aggregate covariate levels that exhibit similar effects on the response. We introduce a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that scales with the number of aggregated levels rather than the original levels, significantly reducing memory requirements and improving computational efficiency. We demonstrate the method’s numerical performance through simulation experiments and its practical applicability through the analysis of NHANES dietary data.

entry.title: Vertex misalignment and changepoint localization in network time series

link.title: Vertex misalignment and changepoint localization in network time series

entry.content: Inference for time series of networks often relies on accurate vertex correspondence between network realizations at different times. In practice, such vertex alignments can be misspecified or unknown. We study the impact of errorful vertex alignment on changepoint localization for dynamic networks through two illustrative models, with the key distinction being whether changepoint information is contained in marginal or joint distributions of the time-varying latent positions. We compare localization techniques ranging from the simple network statistic of average degree to the modern procedure of Euclidean mirrors. Our results demonstrate that understanding the interplay of marginal and joint information in the observed network time series is key to robust network inference.

entry.title: Model-agnostic information transfer and fusion for classification with label noise

link.title: Model-agnostic information transfer and fusion for classification with label noise

entry.content: Label noise presents a fundamental challenge in modern machine learning, especially when large-scale datasets are generated via automated processes. An increasingly common and important data paradigm, particularly in domains like medical imaging, involves learning from a large dataset with coarse, noisy labels supplemented by a small, expert-verified, clean dataset. This setting constitutes a typical information transfer and fusion problem. However, the significant distribution shift between the noisy and clean data violates the core overall parametric similarity assumptions of existing statistical transfer learning methods, while their reliance on parametric models is ill-suited for complex data like images. To address these limitations, this paper develops a generic model-agnostic nonparametric framework for classification with label noise, which applies to a broad class of classifiers. Our approach leverages the small clean dataset to ``purify’’ the large noisy one and carefully manages the remaining ambiguous samples. This framework is underpinned by a rigorous statistical theory. Its empirical performance is demonstrated through simulations and a real-world application to medical image analysis for pneumonia diagnosis.

entry.title: FRESH: Information-Geometric Calibration of Patient-Level Models to Aggregate Evidence

link.title: FRESH: Information-Geometric Calibration of Patient-Level Models to Aggregate Evidence

entry.content: This note introduces FRESH (Fusion of Recent Evidence and Subject Histories), a method for incorporating population-level summary results – published clinical trials, registry summaries, prior natural-history studies, and peer-reviewed indirect comparisons – into predictive models trained on patient-level data. This method provides a principled means of combining both patient-level and aggregate-level data types into a unified data-efficient model for clinical decision making. FRESH assumes access to a generative model trained on patient-level data sources (e.g. clinical trial or real-world data). The method produces patient-level predictions from a re-calibrated model that matches a set of specified aggregate statistics for a target population. This can be understood as a patient-level recapitulation of the aggregate source – with the key property that the recalibration is a minimal perturbation of the original joint distribution in a specific information-geometric sense. The resulting samples can be analyzed directly or combined into a post-training procedure to update the original generative model. This approach enables several applications where rigorously incorporating patient-level data with summary information is valuable, including (i) contextualizing single-arm trial results with respect to recent standard-of-care, (ii) clinical-trial simulations for design and probability-of-technical-success estimation, and (iii) comparative-effectiveness analyses of on-market therapies.

entry.title: Data-Adaptive Multi-Bin Rarefying for Alpha Diversity Association Analysis under Heterogeneous Library Sizes

link.title: Data-Adaptive Multi-Bin Rarefying for Alpha Diversity Association Analysis under Heterogeneous Library Sizes

entry.content: Alpha diversity association analysis is sensitive to heterogeneous library sizes, and overall rarefying to a common depth can either discard many reads from high-depth samples or exclude low-depth samples. We propose MBRarefy, a data-adaptive framework for selecting multi-bin rarefying designs. The method chooses library size cutpoints by minimizing an objective that combines residual within-bin library size dependence with a fragmentation penalty, subject to a minimum bin size constraint. The framework supports both fixed-K and varying-K cutpoint selection. In T-cell receptor (TCR) motivated simulations, the primary fixed-K procedure controlled depth-induced false positives and improved power relative to overall rarefying when group and depth confounding was absent. Applications to TCR immunosequencing and wild baboon gut microbiome data illustrate its ability to reduce residual library size dependence while improving read and sample retention.

entry.title: Perceived vertical and eye level as one orientation process: a closed-form account of the Li-Matin combination rules for egocentric space

link.title: Perceived vertical and eye level as one orientation process: a closed-form account of the Li-Matin combination rules for egocentric space

entry.content: Li and Matin (2005a, 2005b) reported three regularities of the induced visually-perceived vertical (VPV), the direction judged upright. For small tilts, a peripheral line shifts it nearly linearly with tilt, two lines combine nearly linearly, and mirror-image tilts cancel. Each line votes at twice its angle, weighted by its strength. The votes’ vector sum $c_1$ is the first circular moment of the doubled angles; half its angle, $\phi=\tfrac12\arg c_1$, is the induced vertical, a stimulus axis, not the judged upright. This is the orientation order-parameter model (PLUMB). We prove that $c_1$ is, up to a constant factor, the only additive summary of axes (lines without arrowheads) that scales with line strength and turns twice as far as the field rotates. With Li and Matin’s own length gain and no per-configuration fit, the model matches their multiline coefficients in-sample. Their data rule out complete summation but not simple averaging for long lines. But a line’s effect is fourfold (period $90^\circ$): it reverses past $45^\circ$ (Li and Matin, 2005a; Vingerhoets et al., 2009), and near-horizontal lines shift VPV as near-vertical ones do, which $c_1$ forbids. In a two-harmonic fit to Li and Matin’s data, $c_1$ carries an estimated 2–4% of a near-vertical line’s slope and a fourfold term the rest. To first order in tilt, for near-vertical segments, the readout equals the committee rule Shavit, Li, and Matin (2026) fit to eight line-array experiments, with its drives read as concentrations. If the half-fields’ signals are read as sum and difference, perceived eye level (VPEL) is the difference, recovering Shavit, Li, and Matin’s (2013) reversed integration rules; a fourfold term gives the same signals, so this does not single out $c_1$. Re-analysed data (30 observers) show the predicted signs and nulls, an internal check only; the cross-field gain is fitted.

entry.title: Generalised Robust Bayes for Joint Inference of Model and Contamination

link.title: Generalised Robust Bayes for Joint Inference of Model and Contamination

entry.content: Robust generalised Bayesian methods protect parameter inference from contamination but do not generally infer its proportion or identify individual outliers. We propose H"older–Bayes, which applies the H"older divergence to a scaled model to construct a joint generalised posterior over model parameters and the contamination proportion, without specifying an outlier distribution. Each posterior draw flags a corresponding number of observations least compatible with the fitted model; averaging selections propagates joint uncertainty to outlier-detection scores. Under fixed, non-negligible contamination, we establish uniform boundedness of the posterior influence function, a finite-sample $n^{-1/2}$ bound on posterior-averaged excess risk, and a Bernstein–von Mises theorem. Tail overlap between the outlier distribution and the fitted model controls the population risk minimiser’s bias and the associated change in limiting posterior covariance. Interpreting the posterior temperature as an affine volume scaling yields a closed-form, data-driven choice. Simulations and real-data experiments demonstrate robust estimation, contamination-proportion recovery, and posterior-guided data cleaning.

entry.title: Causal Discovery via Transformed Low-Rank Quantile Surfaces

link.title: Causal Discovery via Transformed Low-Rank Quantile Surfaces

entry.content: We propose Low-Rank Quantile Surfaces (LRQS), a bivariate causal model in which, in the causal direction, an unknown monotone transformation of the conditional quantile surface admits a low-rank functional decomposition. LRQS subsumes location-scale noise models and post-nonlinear heteroscedastic noise models, while allowing multiple quantile bases to represent changes beyond location-scale effects. We prove generic identifiability of LRQS: the transformed quantile surface is low rank in the causal direction, whereas reverse representability under the corresponding constraints occurs only for exceptional, fine-tuned cause marginals. We provide a nonparametric causal score using a fitting procedure that alternates between rank-constrained approximation of discretized quantile surfaces and isotonic estimation of the unknown monotone transformation. Experiments on synthetic mechanisms with higher-rank distributional shape variation and strong nonlinear distortions, together with standard bivariate benchmarks, show that LRQS is especially effective when conditional distributional shape or observation distortion goes beyond existing location-scale assumptions.

link.title: Proximal Balancing for Causal Effect Estimation under Unmeasured Confounding

entry.content: Estimating causal effects from observational data is central to science and policy, but the effects are not identified when confounders are unmeasured. Proximal causal inference addresses this problem with proxies of the unmeasured confounders. However, existing proxy-based approaches either designate proxy roles and solve an inverse problem, which is ill-posed and hard to estimate with high-dimensional proxies, or use a latent-variable model, which assumes that the learned latent variable matches the hidden confounder and leaves bias when it does not. To address these challenges, we introduce proximal balancing. It carries the classical idea of covariate balancing to confounders that are observed only through proxies: it learns a low-dimensional summary of the covariates and proxies that makes the treatment groups comparable, and then adjusts for this summary. It needs no designated proxy roles, inverse problem, or latent model. We give identification theory, finite-sample guarantees, and a practical algorithm, PROBE. We demonstrate the method on low-dimensional, high-dimensional, and image proxies and on real-world data.

link.title: Estimating Great Expectations Under Autoregressive Language Models with Potentials

entry.content: Many applications of language models require estimating the expectation of a test functional under the model. Obtaining precise estimates can be computationally expensive. We show how to improve estimation precision by exploiting next-token conditional probabilities available as a by-product of sampling. Our approach uses potentials: real-valued functions of prefixes that induce an additive decomposition of the test functional. We construct a family of estimators parameterized by these potentials and derive conditions for variance reduction. Across applications including entropy estimation, watermark detection, and rare-event probability estimation, our estimators achieve substantial variance reductions relative to Monte Carlo and importance sampling baselines at comparable computational cost.

entry.title: Learning Checklists to Reduce Lottery Effects in Scientific Peer Review

link.title: Learning Checklists to Reduce Lottery Effects in Scientific Peer Review

entry.content: Reviewer lottery error describes error due to a small set of peer reviews attending to only some of the issues with a paper that a larger pool of eligible reviewers would raise. We show this error can be reduced by surfacing a checklist of criticisms learned from a historical review corpus. Our approach generates a tree of checklists representing coarsenings of the atomic review claim space, then selects the coarsening that maximizes a theoretically-motivated measure of correlated agreement among reviewers. We realize this approach with an LLM-assisted pipeline and test it on NeurIPS 2021 and ICLR 2022 review data. In simulated review with LLM reviewers, the learned checklist reduces the mean squared error (MSE) of a three reviewer committee by 58% on NeurIPS and 21% on ICLR, and on both venues the checklist with the highest correlated agreement has the lowest error for committees of three or more. In a human study with 20 participants, the learned NeurIPS checklist lowers the MSE of a paper ranking, measured against the NeurIPS 2021 order, from 0.48 to 0.22.

entry.title: Testing the statistical compatibility of data sets with a common prior

link.title: Testing the statistical compatibility of data sets with a common prior

entry.content: The Parameter Goodness-of-fit (PG) test [hep-ph/0304176] offers a simple test statistic to study the compatibility of different data sets within a given theoretical model. As the prior is imposed for all data sets, they are no longer statistically independent. entry.title: Calibration scoring under dependent seed variables in Cooke’s Classical Model: a Mehler-Hermite design-effect correction

link.title: Calibration scoring under dependent seed variables in Cooke’s Classical Model: a Mehler-Hermite design-effect correction

entry.content: Cooke’s Classical Model scores the statistical accuracy of experts by the $p$-value of a likelihood ratio test that compares the bin frequencies of realized seed variables with nominal probabilities, using a $\chi^2$ reference. This calibration score drives performance-based weights and implicitly assumes independent seed variables, although seeds often share a common driver, such as the same indicator in several regions or periods. Under dependence the statistic converges to a weighted sum of $\chi^2_1$ variables, and positive dependence makes the classical score anti-conservative. Under a Gaussian-copula working model, a Mehler-Hermite expansion gives the long-run covariance of the bin indicators in closed form, defines a design effect and an effective number of seed variables, and shows that the first-order correction coincides with the ad hoc calibration power of existing software. Rao-Scott-type and parametric-bootstrap corrected scores are proposed, together with a restricted maximum likelihood estimator of the nuisance dependence, computed from rank normal scores and invariant to location-scale miscalibration, and a prepivoted bootstrap that propagates its uncertainty. In simulations the classical score rejects up to 68\% of calibrated experts at a nominal 5\% level, whereas the corrected scores remove most of the excess rejection. In 45 published studies, design effects of 1.25-2 shift more than 5\% of the optimized weight in 29-44\% of studies. In three social-science studies with structured seeds, the baseline estimates imply that 18-21 seed variables carry the information of only 11-13 independent ones, although conclusions about individual experts depend on how the dependence is specified.

entry.title: Are New Parties Shut Out of the UK House of Commons?

link.title: Are New Parties Shut Out of the UK House of Commons?

entry.content: In recent years it has been claimed that new political parties are shut out of the UK House of Commons because they are rarely elected. At the same time, general political understanding seems to be that the House of Commons is currently further away from a pure two-party distribution of seats than at any time in the past century, perhaps longer. Although this might seem like a paradox it is possible for both of these things to have credence. We present an analysis that shows that the number of new political parties elected to the House of Commons has been slowly declining over the last century. We illustrate this both by regression and Good-Turing analyses. We also analyse the lifetime and persistence of political parties as well as present metrics that indicate the recent increased political diversity and identify the nadir of diversity in the mid-1960s and early 1970s.

entry.title: Dual-Phase Flow Matching for Probabilistic Source Detection and Measurement in Astronomical Images

link.title: Dual-Phase Flow Matching for Probabilistic Source Detection and Measurement in Astronomical Images

entry.content: Using the largest digital camera ever built, the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) will image over half the night sky. Most astronomical analyses of LSST data operate not on images but on catalogs derived from them: tables of light sources detailing their positions, fluxes (colors and brightnesses), and types (e.g., star, galaxy). At LSST’s imaging depths, light sources often overlap visually, so the configuration of sources in each image is itself uncertain. Nevertheless, LSST’s cataloging pipeline commits to a single source configuration, which can bias downstream analyses. Here, we instead approximate a posterior distribution over source configurations. Our posterior approximation is a continuous-time Markov process (CTMP) fitted by generator matching, an extension of flow matching to non-Euclidean state spaces. This CTMP generates a source configuration in two phases: it detects light sources in the first and measures them in the second. On simulated LSST-like data, the proposed method produces better posterior approximations than five comparison methods: two Markov chain Monte Carlo methods that run thousands of times more slowly at survey scales; two neural posterior estimation methods; and one ablation of the proposed method that lacks the dual-phase structure. Applied to LSST Data Preview 1 (DP1), the first public release of Rubin imaging, the proposed method alone recovers small-scale galaxy clustering in agreement with higher-resolution Hubble imaging and reports uncertainty that remains calibrated against that reference as blending increases. We deliver a probabilistic catalog of the Extended Chandra Deep Field South region, one of the most extensively studied extragalactic fields, and use it to characterize the galaxy color-magnitude distribution.

entry.title: Anytime-Valid Inference in Conjoint Experiments

link.title: Anytime-Valid Inference in Conjoint Experiments

entry.content: Choosing an appropriate sample size is a fundamental challenge in experimental design. This challenge is particularly salient in conjoint experiments, where researchers simultaneously target many estimands whose inferential goals may be reached at different sample sizes. Conventional sample-size calculations address this challenge in an ex ante manner. In large online studies, including many conjoint experiments, data often arrive continuously, allowing researchers to dynamically stop data collection. In such settings, the relevant practical question is not “what sample size should I choose in advance?” but rather, as data accumulate, “have I learned enough yet?” A naive response is to repeatedly inspect conventional confidence intervals and $p$-values, but doing so invalidates their inferential guarantees. We address this challenge by developing a general anytime-valid framework for conjoint experiments that allows continuous monitoring and data-dependent stopping. This framework equips many common conjoint estimands with asymptotic $e$-processes, confidence sequences, and anytime-valid $p$-values, and provides a general recipe for any estimand that can be expressed as a linear contrast of population OLS coefficients. Across common conjoint settings, we demonstrate that anytime-valid inference can yield substantial sample savings relative to fixed-sample designs. The probability of early stopping frequently exceeds 50%, with mean sample savings often surpassing 25%.

entry.title: Estimand frameworks for causal inference in clinical research and regulatory decision making

link.title: Estimand frameworks for causal inference in clinical research and regulatory decision making

entry.content: Causal inference for clinical and regulatory decision making requires a precise definition of the causal estimand, that is, what we want to estimate. Three frameworks are commonly used to describe causal estimands: PICO and its extensions, the target trial framework, and the E9(R1) Addendum of the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH). Because these frameworks were developed by different scientific communities, they operate at different levels of detail, emphasize different aspects of the causal estimand, and use different terminology for closely related concepts. Here we compare the three frameworks and translate across their terminologies. PICO is a compact framework that helps jumpstart a conversation about the causal question, but it does not encode sufficient information to fully characterize a causal estimand. The target trial framework characterizes the causal estimand precisely by specifying the components of the protocol of the randomized trial that would answer the causal question: eligibility criteria, treatment strategies, assignment, outcome, start and end of follow-up, and causal contrast. E9(R1) starts from intercurrent events and lists strategies to address them, some of which describe estimators rather than estimands, or imply estimands that are not relevant to decision makers or cannot be estimated under reasonable assumptions. We argue that the target trial framework subsumes the other two, and we provide a map of the correspondences across the three frameworks.

entry.title: Generalized survival energy models with exogenous covariates for mortality prediction

link.title: Generalized survival energy models with exogenous covariates for mortality prediction

entry.content: We develop a generalized survival energy model that relates mortality to social and economic conditions through a latent energy process. Death occurs when this process first reaches or crosses zero. Environmental covariates enter the coefficients governing depletion, recovery, fluctuations and accumulated damage, yielding lifetime distributions conditional on the environmental path. We derive these distributions for diffusion and inverse Gaussian specifications and describe their numerical evaluation. An application to Japanese male and female mortality data assesses predictive performance against Cairns–Blake–Dowd benchmarks. Conditional on realized environmental paths, the selected inverse Gaussian models achieve small prediction errors comparable to those of the benchmarks. The framework also provides a model-based interpretation of how environmental changes affect mortality through the rate of damage accumulation or the magnitude of energy fluctuations. These interpretations describe conditional statistical relationships rather than causal effects. The resulting models offer a way to study mortality under alternative environmental scenarios while retaining a connection to classical actuarial survival models.

entry.title: Rare-Feature-Adaptive Subsampling for Big Data Regression

link.title: Rare-Feature-Adaptive Subsampling for Big Data Regression

entry.content: Rare binary features cause instability and slow convergence in regression. Subsampling massive datasets may discard observations carrying rare-feature information. We show that rare-feature coefficient convergence rates depend on feature prevalence and the inclusion probabilities assigned to rare observations. This finding motivates subsampling designs that adapt sampling probabilities to feature rarity. We first study optimal rare-census designs, which extend the negative subsampling approach by retaining every rare observation. However, they may face practical constraints. We then propose a computationally efficient rarity-adaptive L-optimal design that incorporates inverse prevalence scaling. Because implementing optimal designs requires pilot estimates whose quality depends on adequate representation of rare features, we propose a balanced design, a one-step rarity-adaptive design based only on binary features. It can be used alone, as a pilot, or combined with designs targeting other objectives. For implementation in two stages, we develop a union-sample estimator that reuses pilot observations while accounting for sample overlap and establish its asymptotic normality. Simulations and applications show improved stability and estimation efficiency over existing methods. One application evaluates designs that jointly protect rare outcomes and rare features.

entry.title: Online Augmented Plug-in Inference for Multi-group Fair Prediction

link.title: Online Augmented Plug-in Inference for Multi-group Fair Prediction

entry.content: Fairness regularization changes both a prediction rule and its sampling uncertainty. We develop online inference for classifiers trained with a covariance penalty on group mean decision scores, a tractable proxy for demographic parity. The framework includes logistic regression and smoothed support-vector machines, with linear regression as a special case targeting equality of group mean predictions. The inferential challenge arises because the fairness operator is estimated from the same stream used to update the predictor. Each observation contributes to its current loss gradient and to subsequent penalty estimates, creating an additional first-order fluctuation in the Polyak–Ruppert average. We derive an asymptotic expansion with harmonic reuse weights and an augmented covariance incorporating score variation, operator variation, and their dependence. Exact fixed-memory recursions yield a consistent covariance estimator and asymptotically valid confidence intervals for the penalized coefficients. Simulation studies assess coverage and interval contraction. Adult-income classification and IPUMS wage regression illustrate coefficient uncertainty and fairness–utility trade-offs, with classification demographic parity evaluated separately through threshold decisions.

entry.title: StochIKM: Automated High-Fidelity Reconstruction of Individual Patient Data from Published Kaplan-Meier Curves

link.title: StochIKM: Automated High-Fidelity Reconstruction of Individual Patient Data from Published Kaplan-Meier Curves

entry.content: Individual patient data are the gold standard for secondary analysis of time-to-event evidence, but they are rarely released, and reconstruction from a published Kaplan-Meier figure could help. Existing methods all claim high fidelity, each judged by whichever agreements it happens to achieve, and each returns a single dataset although the map from figure to data is not bijective. We define fidelity explicitly: a dataset is admissible when it reproduces the risk table exactly, follows the digitized curve to within the image resolution, and respects the printed median, interval and event count. We propose StochIKM, a stochastic algorithm that digitizes the figure with a vision-capable language model and uses the high-fidelity definition as constraints, returning an admissible set of individual patient datasets. A solution is guaranteed to exist whenever the figure has been read correctly, so a failure indicts either the published figure or its digitization. In simulation and in 79 arms from published oncology trials, StochIKM reproduces the published risk tables and medians more closely than LLM-improved IPDfromKM, a high-impact alternative.

entry.title: Uniformly Improved Adaptive Filtering Procedures for Replicability Testing with FWER Control

link.title: Uniformly Improved Adaptive Filtering Procedures for Replicability Testing with FWER Control

entry.content: Identifying signals that replicate across multiple studies is a fundamental challenge in modern data analysis. Partial conjunction (PC) testing addresses this problem by assessing whether a signal is present in at least a specified number of studies. The AdaFilter framework of Wang et al. (2022, Annals of Statistics 50, 1890-1909) improves the power of PC testing through adaptive filtering, but its family-wise error rate (FWER)-controlling procedures rely on conservative Bonferroni corrections at two stages: (i) the construction of PC $p$-values and filtering statistics, and (ii) the multiplicity adjustment used to control the FWER. We show that both stages can be improved using the \v{S}id'ak correction. Under the same independence assumptions as the original AdaFilter framework, our improvements preserve finite-sample FWER control and guarantee at least as many rejections as their Bonferroni counterparts for every realisation of the data. Simulations and a real data analysis demonstrate the practical benefits of these improvements.

link.title: Time-Uniform Dependent Central Limit Theory

entry.content: We establish a near-optimal almost sure invariance principle for nonstationary time series under the functional dependence measure (FDM) framework. This result yields a universal time-uniform dependent central limit theorem, which serves as the basis for anytime-valid inference. In particular, we instantiate the theorem through asymptotic confidence sequences (AsympCSs), time-uniform counterparts of asymptotic confidence intervals obtained via central limit theorems, extending those originally proposed in Waudby-Smith et al. (2024) to time series with serial dependence. We further refine their definition because, as we show, it can admit AsympCSs that fail to achieve the desired asymptotic time-uniform coverage for a broad class of data-generating processes, including independent and identically distributed cases. We address this issue by adding a simple eventual-inclusion condition, which in turn permits more flexible variance estimation, particularly useful in time-series settings. For feasible implementation of AsympCSs, we establish strong consistency of HAC variance estimators under the FDM framework, accommodating a wider range of commonly used bandwidth choices than existing results under mixing conditions. As illustrations, we construct AsympCSs for algorithms with Markovian structure and time-series-based causal estimands.

entry.title: Using Temporal Replication and Partial Pooling to Improve Practical Identifiability in Presence-Only Poisson Point Process Models

link.title: Using Temporal Replication and Partial Pooling to Improve Practical Identifiability in Presence-Only Poisson Point Process Models

entry.content: Species distribution models based on thinned point processes are now commonly used in ecology to analyze presence-only data collected through citizen science, including in spatio-temporal frameworks. A key challenge in these models is the separation of the ecological process from the observation process, which raises identifiability issues. Here, we investigate the theoretical and practical identifiability of a thinned Poisson point process model. We show that, with a log link for ecological intensity and a logit link for observation probability, the model can be structurally identifiable under simple conditions, provided that observation probability varies spatially. We then evaluate the benefits of using temporal replication within a spatio-temporal framework to improve estimation when ecological intensity and observation probability are weakly separated. We quantify these benefits through simulations. The results highlight persistent practical identifiability problems affecting the ecological and observation intercepts, especially when observation probabilities are low. However, in a spatio-temporal model with partial pooling, these parameters are estimated more accurately than in a single-year model, even when only a short time period is considered. Temporal replication also improves estimation of parameters shared across years. Finally, we illustrate the use of such a spatio-temporal model through a study of coypu (Myocastor coypus) distribution in Occitanie, France. Overall, our results show that temporal replication can partially alleviate practical identifiability problems in presence-only point process models when independent data sources are unavailable.

entry.title: Asynchronous, Generation-Free ABC: Streaming AMIS Reweighting for Heterogeneous Simulator Workloads on HPC

link.title: Asynchronous, Generation-Free ABC: Streaming AMIS Reweighting for Heterogeneous Simulator Workloads on HPC

entry.content: Approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) enables Bayesian inference for models with intractable likelihoods by estimating parameter posterior distributions from simulated data. Sequential ABC methods improve sampling efficiency by iteratively adapting the proposal distribution toward regions of high posterior probability. However, these methods typically operate in generations, where each generation must wait for its slowest simulation before the next can begin. On a parallel machine, this synchronization barrier leaves workers idle and reduces throughput, particularly when simulation runtimes vary substantially. We introduce a generation-free ABC sampler that updates its proposal when simulation results arrive and sends a new candidate to each available worker. The proposal is based on the best particles evaluated so far. To estimate the posterior, we reuse the full history and reweight particles against a reconstructed mixture of sampling proposals. We show how errors in approximating the mixture of sampling proposals affect the estimated posterior and establish consistency for the smooth-ABC posterior when the approximation becomes asymptotically exact. In our experiments, the method achieves well-calibrated posterior estimates where a pyABC baseline with the same kernel and bandwidth schedule under-covers. From the asynchronous run’s timing alone, we predict how much a synchronization barrier would slow the sampler. These predictions agree with measured synchronization penalties ranging from 1.2x to 400x. On a Cellular Potts tissue simulator, the asynchronous sampler completes 2.1-2.4x as many evaluations as pyABC in the same hour, and the discrepancy threshold for its best 100 evaluations is 4.1x smaller. With the starting bandwidth set from prior-predictive discrepancies, it also produces a more concentrated two-parameter posterior with a larger effective sample size than pyABC.

entry.title: Sequential Entropic Optimal Transport for Bayesian Inverse Problems via Multilevel Monte Carlo

link.title: Sequential Entropic Optimal Transport for Bayesian Inverse Problems via Multilevel Monte Carlo

entry.content: We consider the problem of Bayesian estimation associated to inverse problems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs). In most cases of practical interest, one must use numerical solvers to implement computational methods based on Monte Carlo methods. This inevitably leads to an adaptation of multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) methods to reduce computational efforts to achieve a pre-specified mean square error (MSE). MLMC is based on sampling coupled versions of Bayesian posteriors associated to increasingly precise numerical solves of the PDE. In this article we present a novel method to implement MLMC based upon sequential entropic optimal transport couplings learned with light Schr"odinger bridges, and correct the transport with Metropolis–Hastings steps that preserve the pairing. We bound the mean square error associated to a version of our new estimation method and show, for an elliptic inverse problem, that to achieve a MSE of $\mathcal{O}(\delta^2)$ ($\delta >0$) one can have an optimal cost of $\mathcal{O}(\delta^{-2})$. The results feature explicit bounds on the effect of the fitted transport and of the Metropolis–Hastings correction. From a numerical perspective, on elliptic, Darcy-flow and Navier-Stokes problems, the method reduces the variance of the most precise solver by a factor of five to ten and is faster than multilevel sequential Monte Carlo [arXiv:1503.07259] at tight accuracies.

entry.title: Lifting PCA in the Wasserstein Space

link.title: Lifting PCA in the Wasserstein Space

entry.content: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a fundamental tool for statistical dimension reduction, yet no canonical extension to distribution-valued data has emerged within the framework of optimal transport. While Wasserstein barycenters and Wasserstein least-squares regression provide canonical liftings of Euclidean averaging and linear regression in the Wasserstein space, an analogous principle for PCA has remained unexplored. In this paper, we introduce Lifted PCA, a canonical extension of Euclidean PCA to Wasserstein space, obtained through the framework of lifting functionals in the space of probability measures by convex extension. Starting from the classical variational formulations of PCA on the Stiefel and Grassmann manifolds, we derive two equivalent minimization problems over probability measures supported on these manifolds that correspond to Wasserstein barycenters with generalized costs. We establish an exact analogue of the equivalence between the Stiefel and Grassmann formulations of Euclidean PCA, preserving PCA’s original variational structure under lifting. We further derive dual formulations and optimality conditions, and establish equivalences with multimarginal optimal transport and matching-for-teams problems. We also establish statistical consistency for empirical estimators and develop computational algorithms based on the Wasserstein barycenter formulation over the Stiefel manifold. Whereas Euclidean PCA summarizes vectors through projections onto an optimal low-dimensional linear subspace, Lifted PCA summarizes probability distributions through an optimal probability measure supported on multiple low-dimensional subspaces. Numerical experiments on distributional datasets illustrate the practical performance of the proposed methodology and its benefits for distributional data analysis.

entry.title: Optimally Emulating Smooth Functions for Bayesian Analyses

link.title: Optimally Emulating Smooth Functions for Bayesian Analyses

entry.content: For Bayesian analyses aimed at constraining the parameter space of computationally expensive models by comparison with heterogeneous data sets, model emulators play a pivotal role. Model emulators enable searches through high-dimensional parameter spaces, searches which might otherwise require millions of full model runs. Here, an emulation strategy is presented based on the assumption that the model output can be well described by a polynomial expansion with all terms being independent of one another and with higher order terms being given decreasing weights according to a convergence parameter. It is found that if the expansion’s form is constrained to being invariant to rotation and translation of the parameter space that the polynomial form becomes equivalent to that of a Gaussian process emulator using a correlation kernel with a Gaussian form. In the limit that the function is smooth, quantified by a convergence parameter, $\Lambda$, it is found that rather few training points are required to reproduce the full model and provide a good estimate of its uncertainty. An accuracy metric is defined based on an average of the expected uncertainty over the prior before training data are actually gathered. Analytic expressions for the expected accuracy are provided based solely on an expected value of $\Lambda$ and the location of the training points. This enables a tenable optimized placement of training points, which is shown to be significantly superior to random placement or that from Latin hyper-cube sampling. Examples of optimized placement are provided, and the accuracy is studied as a function of various variables, such as the number of model parameters, the number of training points, and the convergence parameter.

entry.title: Bayesian Comparison of Covid Origins Hypotheses

link.title: Bayesian Comparison of Covid Origins Hypotheses

entry.content: Applying standard Bayesian methods to the most reliably known unclassified facts about the Covid epidemic allows crude estimation of the odds for research-related vs. purely zoonotic origins. Here a broadly inclusive zoonotic hypothesis is compared with a rather specific subset of the research-related hypothesis defined by known prior work and grant proposals. The important observations are the type of virus, the city of the first outbreak, the lack of known prior hosts, the anomalous early pattern of evolution, and two specific features of the viral sequence. The resulting odds strongly favor research. The odds remain fairly strong under inclusion of uncertainties in prior odds.

entry.title: Mastering Model Fit: Applications of the InterModel Vigorish for Interpretable Machine Learning

link.title: Mastering Model Fit: Applications of the InterModel Vigorish for Interpretable Machine Learning

entry.content: Accuracy alone gives little information about which features or model components improve probabilistic fit, which outcomes benefit, or how fit changes during training. We introduce the InterModel Vigorish (IMV) into the Machine Intelligence space in order to express differences in fit as an expected betting advantage over a reference model. SHAP-IMV attributes gains to features through Shapley-weighted subset comparisons, Multi-IMV evaluates one-vs-rest and pairwise class discrimination, and Ablate-IMV assesses architectural components and feature groups by ablation. We evaluate these applications over ten random seeds using tabular data, images, sensor sequences, and graphs. Feature rankings vary across estimators. High one-vs-rest accuracy can accompany negligible improvement over a null, while ablation can preserve or improve fit under a fixed training budget. On six graph-classification benchmarks, we time-profile IMV over 200 training epochs, reporting seed means and ranges. The open-source imvpy library and accompanying notebooks provide code to replicate our work and to use the IMV more widely.

entry.title: Flowz: When Does Learning Forecast Errors Add Value? Conditional Flow Matching for Financial Price Forecasts

link.title: Flowz: When Does Learning Forecast Errors Add Value? Conditional Flow Matching for Financial Price Forecasts

entry.content: Learning a forecasting model’s errors offers a modular way to improve its predictive distribution while retaining its underlying dynamics. We study this approach with Flowz, a conditional flow model of direct multi-step price-level residuals fitted using random features and ridge regression. Each EWMA, ARIMA, ARFIMA, and structural baseline is compared with a Gaussian residual location-scale control and a conditional Flowz extension. The experiment uses 24 US stocks selected across four liquidity-volatility strata, 104 common forecast origins, horizons of 5, 10, 20, 40, 80, and 160 trading observations, and three fit seeds. Marginal CRPS is the primary score. At farther horizons, Flowz reduces mean CRPS by 30.7% against EWMA and 24.0% against its Gaussian residual control. The EWMA improvement holds at each fit seed and exceeds the Gaussian control for all 24 stocks in the far band. The ARIMA, ARFIMA, and structural extensions worsen both comparators. Conditional residual learning is therefore useful for the drifting EWMA specification in this experiment, with gains concentrated at longer horizons.

entry.title: CAQ: Clustered Asymptotically Anytime-Valid Quantile Treatment Effects for Online Experiments

link.title: CAQ: Clustered Asymptotically Anytime-Valid Quantile Treatment Effects for Online Experiments

entry.content: Confidence sequences let an experiment be monitored continuously without inflating error, but the existing constructions for quantiles assume that observations arrive independently. In online experiments this rarely holds: randomization assigns users, while the metric is computed over the many correlated events each user generates, so intervals built for independent data are too narrow and miss the truth more often than their nominal rate allows. We propose CAQ, a confidence sequence for a quantile that is both robust to this within-user dependence and valid at arbitrary stopping times, together with a sequential test for the difference in a quantile between two treatment arms. The width adapts to the dependence actually present, widening beyond the independent-data benchmark only when correlation within users is strong. In simulations, CAQ is the only method we tested that holds both coverage and false-positive rate at their nominal levels across clustering strengths and heavy-tailed data, while the fixed-horizon baseline fails under continuous monitoring and the independence-assuming sequential baseline fails as within-user correlation grows.

entry.title: When Windowed Anderson Acceleration Converges Faster

link.title: When Windowed Anderson Acceleration Converges Faster

entry.content: Windowed Anderson acceleration AA($m$) combines at most $m+1$ recent iterates by least squares. For a real affine contraction $x\mapsto Wx+b$ with $q=|W| \in(0,1)$, we determine exactly when AA($m$) converges from every starting point with an asymptotic factor below $q$. We give a polynomial criterion for this improvement and an equivalent spectral condition: there is no probability distribution on the phases of the eigenvalues of modulus $q$ whose first $m$ cosine moments are $q,q^2,\ldots,q^m$. If such a distribution exists, we construct a starting point from which AA($m$) reproduces fixed-point iteration at every step. Otherwise, over a fixed number of consecutive steps, every run contracts the residual norm by a common factor strictly smaller than the corresponding power of $q$. The polynomial criterion also gives explicit convergence-rate bounds with constants independent of the dimension. When $q$ equals the spectral radius, this characterizes improvement over the asymptotic convergence factor of fixed-point iteration. For general affine contractions, the asymptotic factor never exceeds the numerical radius of $W$, and a related moment condition gives a uniform upper bound strictly below that radius.

entry.title: Technical Report: Causal ANOVA Applied to COMPAS

link.title: Technical Report: Causal ANOVA Applied to COMPAS

entry.content: This report applies Causal ANOVA to the COMPAS recidivism prediction dataset to study how demographic variables contribute to variation in two-year recidivism outcomes. Using a directed acyclic graph (DAG) to encode causal assumptions, we estimate counterfactual explainability scores for Race, Sex, and Age Category. We then examine whether the explanatory roles of Race and Sex change after conditioning on age group. The results suggest that Age Category explains the largest share of variation in the full causal model. After conditioning on age, Sex explainability is highest among younger defendants and declines with age, while Race explainability increases with age and is most pronounced among older defendants. As a complementary analysis, we use logistic regression models to interpret the demographic patterns suggested by the Causal ANOVA results. We provide a Python package of Causal ANOVA at https://github.com/devonxiong/causal-anova.

entry.title: Testing for genetic interactions in complex disease with distance correlation

link.title: Testing for genetic interactions in complex disease with distance correlation

entry.content: Understanding epistasis (genetic interaction) may shed some light on the genomic basis of common diseases, including disorders of maximum interest due to their high socioeconomic burden, like schizophrenia. Distance correlation is an association measure that characterizes general statistical independence between random variables, not only the linear one. Here, we propose distance correlation as a novel tool for the detection of epistasis from case-control data of single-nucleotide polymorphisms. On the methodological side, we highlight the derivation of the explicit asymptotic null distribution of the test statistic. We show that this is the only way to obtain enough computational speed for the method to be used in practice, in a scenario where the resampling techniques found in the literature are impractical. Our simulations show satisfactory calibration of significance, as well as comparable or better power than existing methodology. We conclude with the application of our technique to a schizophrenia genetics dataset, obtaining biologically sound insights.

entry.title: Quasi-Score Matching Estimation for Spatial Autoregressive Model with Random Weights Matrix and Regressors

link.title: Quasi-Score Matching Estimation for Spatial Autoregressive Model with Random Weights Matrix and Regressors

entry.content: With the rapid advancements in technology for data collection, the application of the spatial autoregressive (SAR) model has become increasingly prevalent in real-world analysis, particularly when dealing with large datasets. However, the commonly used quasi-maximum likelihood estimation (QMLE) for the SAR model is not computationally scalable to handle the data with a large size. In addition, when establishing the asymptotic properties of the parameter estimators of the SAR model, both weights matrix and regressors are assumed to be nonstochastic in classical spatial econometrics, which is perhaps not realistic in real applications. Motivated by the machine learning literature, this paper proposes quasi-score matching estimation for the SAR model. This new estimation approach is developed based on the likelihood, but significantly reduces the computational complexity of the QMLE. The asymptotic properties of parameter estimators under the random weights matrix and regressors are established, which provides a new theoretical framework for the asymptotic inference of the SAR-type models. The usefulness of the quasi-score matching estimation and its asymptotic inference is illustrated via extensive simulation studies and a case study of an anti-conflict social network experiment for middle school students.
