entry.title: Statistical inference for a multiscale stochastic model of enzyme kinetics via propagation of chaos

link.title: Statistical inference for a multiscale stochastic model of enzyme kinetics via propagation of chaos

entry.content: We study a class of Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs) with jumps modeling multistage Michaelis–Menten enzyme kinetics, in which a substrate is sequentially transformed into a product via a cascade of intermediate complexes. These networks are typically high-dimensional and exhibit multiscale behavior with a strong coupling between different components, posing substantial analytical and computational challenges. In particular, the problem of statistical inference of reaction rates is significantly difficult and becomes even more intricate when direct observations of system states are unavailable and only a random sample of product formation times is observed. We address this problem in two stages. First, in a suitable scaling regime consistent with the Quasi-Steady State Approximation (QSSA), we rigorously establish a stochastic averaging principle yielding a reduced model for the product-substrate dynamics. Guided by the reduced-order dynamics, we next construct a novel Interacting Particle System (IPS) that approximates the product-substrate process at the particle level. This IPS plays a pivotal role in the inference methodology, and we prove several non-asymptotic bounds and limiting results for this system. These results facilitate the construction of an estimator based on a product-form approximate likelihood requiring only a random sample of product formation times. This approach does not need access to the system states, and we rigorously prove consistency of the estimator.

entry.title: Feature Selection for Latent Factor Models

link.title: Feature Selection for Latent Factor Models

entry.content: Feature selection is crucial for pinpointing relevant features in high-dimensional datasets, mitigating the ‘curse of dimensionality,’ and enhancing machine learning performance. Traditional feature selection methods for classification use data from all classes to select features for each class. This paper explores feature selection methods that select features for each class separately, using class models based on low-rank generative methods and introducing a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) feature selection criterion. This novel approach offers a theoretically sound guarantee of feature recovery under specific assumptions and has been demonstrated to outperform some existing feature selection methods on standard classification datasets. Additionally, it can be easily applied in a class-incremental learning setup, yielding performance comparable to that of some current methods.

entry.title: Direct Inversion for Chi-Square Sampling, the Squared Bessel Process, and Applications

link.title: Direct Inversion for Chi-Square Sampling, the Squared Bessel Process, and Applications

entry.content: In this paper we derive a new direct inversion method to simulate squared Bessel processes. Since the transition probability of these processes can be represented by a non-central chi-square distribution, we construct an efficient and accurate algorithm to simulate non-central chi-square variables. In this method, the dimension of the squared Bessel process, equivalently the degrees of freedom of the chi-square distribution, is treated as a variable. We therefore use a two-dimensional Chebyshev expansion to approximate the inverse function of the central chi-square distribution with one variable being the degrees of freedom. The method is accurate and efficient for any value of degrees of freedom including the computationally challenging case of small values. One advantage of the method is that noncentral chi-square samples can be generated for a whole range of values of degrees of freedom using the same Chebyshev coefficients. This property is especially useful in model calibration. The squared Bessel process is a building block for the well-known Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) processes, which can be generated from squared Bessel processes through time change and linear transformation. Our direct inversion method thus allows the efficient and accurate simulation of these processes, which are used as models in a wide variety of applications.

entry.title: Estimation of Treatment Effects Under Nonstationarity via the Truncated Policy Gradient Estimator

link.title: Estimation of Treatment Effects Under Nonstationarity via the Truncated Policy Gradient Estimator

entry.content: Randomized experiments (or A/B tests) are widely used to evaluate interventions in dynamic systems such as recommendation platforms, marketplaces, and digital health. In these settings, interventions affect both current and future system states, so estimating the global average treatment effect (GATE) requires accounting for temporal dynamics, which is especially challenging in the presence of nonstationarity; existing approaches suffer from high bias, high variance, or both. In this paper, we address this challenge via the novel Truncated Policy Gradient (TPG) estimator, which replaces instantaneous outcomes with short-horizon outcome trajectories. The estimator admits a policy gradient interpretation: it is a truncation of the first-order approximation to the GATE, yielding explicit bias and variance bounds in nonstationary Markovian settings. For a fixed truncation size, we establish a central limit theorem and, under an additional mean-stability condition, the consistency of a variance estimator for nonstationary single-trajectory data. We validate our theory with two real-world case studies. The results show that relative to existing approaches, a well-calibrated TPG estimator can achieve a favorable balance between bias and variance in nonstationary settings, highlighting the value of the policy-gradient perspective for designing effective estimators under complex dynamics.

entry.title: Inference of Hierarchical Core-Periphery Structure in Temporal Networks

link.title: Inference of Hierarchical Core-Periphery Structure in Temporal Networks

entry.content: Networks can have various types of mesoscale structures. One such structure is core–periphery structure, which consists of sets of densely-connected core nodes and sets of sparsely-connected peripheral nodes. Core nodes are connected densely to other core nodes and are potentially connected densely to peripheral nodes, which are connected sparsely to other nodes. There has been much research on core–periphery structure in time-independent networks, but few core–periphery detection methods have been developed for time-dependent (i.e., temporal") networks. Using a multilayer-network representation of temporal networks and an inference approach that employs stochastic block models, we generalize a recent method for detecting hierarchical core--periphery structure \cite{Polanco23} from time-independent networks to temporal networks. In contrast toonion-like’’ nested core–periphery structures (where each node is assigned to a group according to how deeply it is nested in a network’s core), hierarchical core–periphery structures encompass networks with nested structures, tree-like structures (where any two groups must either be disjoint or have one group as a strict subset of the other group), and general non-nested mesoscale structures (where the group assignments of nodes do not have to be nested in any way). To perform statistical inference and thereby identify hierarchical core–periphery structure, we use a Markov-chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approach. We illustrate our method for detecting hierarchical core–periphery structure in one synthetic temporal network and two real-world temporal networks, and we discuss the structures that we identify in these networks.

entry.title: Weak Factor Analysis via Temporally Weighted PCA

link.title: Weak Factor Analysis via Temporally Weighted PCA

entry.content: Principal component analysis (PCA) is arguably the most widely used approach for large-dimensional factor analysis. While it is effective when the factors are sufficiently strong, it can be inconsistent when the factors are weak and/or the noise has complex dependence structure. We argue that the inconsistency often stems from bias and introduce a general approach to restore consistency. Specifically, we propose a general weighting scheme for PCA and show that suitable weights can restore consistency for much weaker factors under the dependent-noise structures allowed by our model. Under the stronger signal-to-noise conditions needed for inference, we also establish asymptotic normality of the loading and factor estimators. While an oracle weighting matrix may require knowledge about the factors and covariance of the idiosyncratic noise that are not known a priori, we develop an agnostic approach to adaptively choose from a large class of weighting matrices that can be viewed as PCA for weighted linear combinations of auto-covariances among the observations. Theoretical and numerical results demonstrate the merits of our methodology over the usual PCA and other recently developed techniques for large-dimensional approximate factor models.

entry.title: RAPSEM: Identifying Latent Mediators Without Sequential Ignorability via a Rank-Preserving Structural Equation Model

link.title: RAPSEM: Identifying Latent Mediators Without Sequential Ignorability via a Rank-Preserving Structural Equation Model

entry.content: Standard structural equation models (SEMs) are often used to identify latent mediators. However, valid inference typically relies on the strong, frequently violated Sequential Ignorability assumption. We introduce the Rank-Preserving Structural Equation Model (RAPSEM), which increases robustness through G-estimation while maintaining the measurement model’s integrity through a two-stage method of moments (2SMM) for factor score corrections. RAPSEM replaces the no unmeasured mediator-outcome confounding with the weaker no unobserved effect modification assumption. By leveraging treatment randomization, RAPSEM achieves identification in a manner equivalent to instrumental variable estimation through structurally emerging instruments. Specifically, identification relies on treatment-covariate interactions that influence the mediator but have no direct effect on the outcome, allowing researchers to utilize natural heterogeneity in treatment response as a testable source of identification. We provide a robustness assessment for the core identifying assumption and establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the resulting estimator. Simulation studies demonstrate that RAPSEM remains unbiased under unobserved confounding, whereas standard SEM yields biased results. RAPSEM achieves reasonable power for sample sizes above 500, depending on the strength of the structural instruments. The method is implemented in the accompanying rapsem R package, and its practical utility is illustrated through an empirical example from educational research. The code is available at https://github.com/PsychometricsMZ/RAPSEM.

entry.title: Bayesian Nonparametric Dynamical Clustering of Time Series

link.title: Bayesian Nonparametric Dynamical Clustering of Time Series

entry.content: We present a method that models the evolution of an unbounded number of time series clusters by switching among an unknown number of regimes with linear dynamics. We develop a Bayesian non-parametric approach using a hierarchical Dirichlet process as a prior on the parameters of a Switching Linear Dynamical System and a Gaussian process prior to model the statistical variations in amplitude and temporal alignment within each cluster. By modeling the evolution of time series patterns, the method avoids unnecessary proliferation of clusters in a principled manner. We perform inference by formulating a variational lower bound for off-line and on-line scenarios, enabling efficient learning through optimization. We illustrate the versatility and effectiveness of the approach through several case studies of electrocardiogram analysis using publicly available databases.

entry.title: Discovering Causal Relationships Between Time Series With Spatial Structure

link.title: Discovering Causal Relationships Between Time Series With Spatial Structure

entry.content: Causal discovery is the subfield of causal inference concerned with estimating the structure of cause-and-effect relationships in a system of interrelated variables, as opposed to quantifying the strength or describing the form of causal effects. As interest in causal discovery builds in fields such as ecology, public health, and environmental sciences, where data are regularly collected with spatial and temporal structures, approaches must evolve to manage autocorrelation and complex confounding. As it stands, the few proposed causal discovery algorithms for spatiotemporal data require summarizing across locations, ignore spatial autocorrelation, and/or scale poorly to high dimensions. Here, we introduce our framework to extend time-series causal discovery to systems with spatial structure. Building upon work on causal discovery across contexts and methods for handling spatial confounding in causal effect estimation, we prove the soundness and completeness of our extension in the large sample limit. We close by discussing the feasibility of the framework, outlining remaining gaps in the literature, and identifying directions for future research.

entry.title: Source apportionment of air pollution burden using geometric non-negative matrix factorization and high-throughput multi-pollutant air sensor data in Curtis Bay, Baltimore, USA

link.title: Source apportionment of air pollution burden using geometric non-negative matrix factorization and high-throughput multi-pollutant air sensor data in Curtis Bay, Baltimore, USA

entry.content: Air sensor networks provide hyperlocal, high-frequency data on multiple pollutants, but unlike speciated particulate matter (PM) measurements, they lack direct chemical signatures for source identification. However, these networks collect data at high temporal resolution and multiple spatial locations, creating new opportunities to interpret latent factors through their relationships with spatial proximity to known origins, temporal patterns, and meteorology. We analyze 451,946 one-minute air sensor records from Curtis Bay (Baltimore, USA; October 2022 - June 2023), covering size-resolved PM, black carbon (BC), carbon monoxide (CO), nitric oxide (NO), and nitrogen dioxide (NO2), using a geometric non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) approach that scales to large datasets and yields provably unique factor attribution percentages. Three stable latent factors emerge with converging evidence toward recognizable source categories: Factor 1 explains $>$ 70% of fine and coarse PM and $\sim$30% of BC; Factor 2 dominates CO and contributes $\sim$70% of BC, NO, and NO2; Factor 3 is specific to the larger PM fractions, PM10 to PM40. Regression analyses of the estimated factor intensities with wind direction and bulldozer activity at a nearby coal terminal and a case study on a known bulldozer incident link Factors 1 and 3 to the coal terminal. Extreme-intensity episodes from Factors 1 and 3 averaged $\sim$33 and $\sim$24 minutes per day at the site nearest the coal terminal, attenuating with distance. Factor 2 reflects diurnal traffic patterns. Together, these results show that dense air sensor networks paired with the geometric NMF method can move community air monitoring beyond pollution detection toward identifying likely source categories and informing actionable mitigation strategies.

entry.title: A spatiotemporal Bayesian hierarchical model of heat-related mortality in Catalonia, Spain (2012–2022): The role of environmental and socioeconomic modifiers

link.title: A spatiotemporal Bayesian hierarchical model of heat-related mortality in Catalonia, Spain (2012–2022): The role of environmental and socioeconomic modifiers

entry.content: Background: Extreme heat is a major public health risk, yet its relationship with mortality may be confounded or modified by air pollution and social determinants. Objectives: We aimed to quantify the effects of extreme maximum temperatures and heatwaves on daily mortality in Catalonia (2012–2022), and to assess the modifying and confounding roles of air pollutants and socioeconomic factors. Methods: We conducted a time–series ecological study across 379 basic health areas (ABS) during summer months. Mortality data from the Spanish National Statistics Institute were linked with meteorological and air pollution data. A hierarchical Bayesian spatiotemporal model, incorporating structured and unstructured random effects, was used to account for spatial and temporal dependencies, as well as observed socioeconomic confounders. Results: In total, 730,634 deaths occurred, with 216,989 in summer. Extreme heat alone was not independently associated with mortality, as its effect was fully confounded by high ozone levels and partly by socioeconomic indicators. Ozone concentrations ($\ge 120 \mu g/m^3$) significantly increased mortality risk, especially among individuals aged $\ge 85$ years. Greater income inequality and higher proportions of older residents also amplified vulnerability. Conclusion: Mortality risks from extreme heat in Catalonia were strongly influenced by ozone levels and social determinants. Adaptation strategies should address both compound environmental exposures together with socioeconomic vulnerability to better protect older and disadvantaged populations.

entry.title: Beyond Missing Data: Questionnaire Response Uncertainty as an Early Digital Sign of Dementia-Related Vulnerability

link.title: Beyond Missing Data: Questionnaire Response Uncertainty as an Early Digital Sign of Dementia-Related Vulnerability

entry.content: Explicit “Do not know” responses are treated as missing data, although their accumulation may encode uncertainty. We analysed 502,234 UK Biobank participants to test associations between response uncertainty and incident dementia-related diagnoses. Compared with participants giving 0–1 such responses, those giving more than seven had higher risks of the dementia-related disease composite (hazard ratio 1.62, 95% confidence interval 1.50–1.74), Alzheimer’s disease (1.63, 1.48–1.79), and vascular dementia (1.63, 1.42–1.86) after multivariable adjustment. Associations were approximately linear, persisted after a two-year lag, and were directionally reproduced in Scotland and Wales. Polygenic risk scores minimally attenuated these associations. Domain, molecular, and chronic-disease analyses placed response uncertainty within a broader multisystem vulnerability phenotype. Here, we show that explicit response uncertainty provides a scalable behavioural marker of subsequent dementia-related risk.

entry.title: Accuracy of Uniform Inference on Fine Grid Points

link.title: Accuracy of Uniform Inference on Fine Grid Points

entry.content: Uniform confidence bands are widely used to quantify uncertainty about unknown functions in nonparametric inference. Although various methods, including the multiplier bootstrap, have been developed and theoretically justified, practical implementations typically replace the supremum over a continuum by the maximum over a finite evaluation grid. This paper investigates how this discretization affects coverage accuracy and how fine the evaluation grid must be to ensure valid uniform inference. We first illustrate through simulations of a kernel-based nonparametric estimator that coarse grids can substantially reduce uniform coverage. Surprisingly, increasing the sample size can worsen coverage on a fixed coarse grid, even as the remaining approximation error on the grid decreases. We then derive general upper bounds on the coverage probability and coverage error of uniform confidence bands based on multiplier-bootstrap critical values on the finite grid points, separating discretization error from the remaining approximation error on the grid. For local empirical processes arising from kernel smoothing, we establish primitive conditions under which coverage converges to zero even when the number of grid points diverges, and conditions ensuring asymptotically nominal coverage. The latter results yield rate-sharp grid resolution requirements in terms of the bandwidth. Furthermore, we derive an explicit leading constant in the bound on coverage error and develop a quantitative grid selection rule for a user-specified discretization tolerance level, which can be implemented through a simple one-dimensional search.

entry.title: Combining e-values using demi-supermartingales

link.title: Combining e-values using demi-supermartingales

entry.content: We present a new method for combining e-variables through demi-supermartingales, which settles an old conjecture in the literature on nonparametric mean testing. It also provides an explicit concentration bound for a certain Kullback–Leibler-type statistic arising in the stochastic multi-armed bandit literature. All of these combination results hold for independent e-variables as well as for the class of co-valid e-variables, whose dependence structure lies somewhere between independence and sequential validity. The results are further generalized to compound e-variables. The proofs proceed by analyzing elementary symmetric polynomials and their behavior as nonnegative demi-supermartingales.

entry.title: Unsupervised Learning Under a General Semiparametric Clusterwise Elliptical Distribution: Efficient Estimation, Optimal Clustering, and Consistent Cluster Selection

link.title: Unsupervised Learning Under a General Semiparametric Clusterwise Elliptical Distribution: Efficient Estimation, Optimal Clustering, and Consistent Cluster Selection

entry.content: A general semiparametric clusterwise elliptical distribution is introduced for assessing how latent cluster structure shapes continuous outcomes. Using a subjectwise representation, cluster-specific mean vectors are estimated by minimizing a weighted sum of squares criterion augmented with a separation penalty. An initialization scheme based on iterative Mahalanobis reassignment and a computational algorithm with guaranteed convergence accompany the estimation procedure. Under the localization conditions, the separation penalty criterion admits a local oracle property, and the corresponding localized partition recovers the realized latent cluster partition. The practical iterative Mahalanobis reassignment does not impose these truth-centered neighborhoods and is evaluated separately through numerical studies. The resulting first-phase partition seeds a second phase of pseudo-likelihood-based estimation and cluster reassignment. A semiparametric information criterion is also proposed for selecting the number of clusters. Monte Carlo simulations identify settings in which the proposed procedures improve on the evaluated parametric benchmarks, while additional experiments reveal sensitivity to cluster imbalance and departures from ellipticity. Applications illustrate the resulting customer and patient profiles.

entry.title: Nonparametric Identification and Estimation of Causal Effects on Latent Outcomes

link.title: Nonparametric Identification and Estimation of Causal Effects on Latent Outcomes

entry.content: How can we conduct causal inference when the outcome of interest is latent and imperfectly measured by multiple indicators? We develop a nonparametric framework for identifying and estimating average treatment effects on latent outcomes in randomized experiments. Researchers commonly aggregate multiple outcome indicators into a summary measure before estimating treatment effects. We identify a fundamental but often overlooked comparability problem arising from this practice: adding, removing, or replacing indicators can alter the causal estimand. We formalize this problem and show that commonly used procedures generally fail to preserve comparability across measurement sets. To address this problem, we propose a design-based approach that uses nonparametric bridge functions. We further characterize the semiparametric efficiency bound, construct an efficient estimator, and establish necessary and sufficient conditions under which additional measurements yield strict efficiency gains. We illustrate our approach through an application to the Hajj visa lottery. Our framework provides practical guidance for measurement design, identification, and efficient causal estimation with latent outcomes.

link.title: Neural Posterior Estimation for Spatial Individual-Level Epidemic Models

entry.content: Spatial individual-level models (ILMs) provide a flexible framework for modeling infectious disease transmission across populations with known locations. entry.title: Computing the final epidemic size distributions of a multi-type Galton–Watson process

link.title: Computing the final epidemic size distributions of a multi-type Galton–Watson process

entry.content: The Galton–Watson process (GWP) is a discrete-time branching process model that provides a powerful tool for analyzing epidemic data and estimating key epidemiological parameters such as the basic reproduction number. When used with surveillance-based cluster size data, the GWP can also elicit information about the extent of transmission heterogeneity, even when each transmission process is not directly observable. When cluster size distribution data are available, the parameters that govern the transmission can be statistically inferred by using the probability mass function that corresponds to the observed cluster size data. For multi-type GWPs, however, real-world applications remain limited, possibly because of the absence of conceptually and practically straightforward approaches for deriving the closed-form solution of the final size distribution. In the present study, we propose a framework for computing the final size distribution of multi-type GWPs, using a method for the choice of the Cauchy integral contour. We provide examples of how our framework can be applied to both simulated data and real-world data of Middle East respiratory syndrome, and discuss potential pitfalls surrounding the identifiability of parameters for statistical inference when using likelihoods that are not conditioned on extinction.

entry.title: A Deep Zero-Inflated Model of North Atlantic Right Whale Presence To Support Blue Economy Management

link.title: A Deep Zero-Inflated Model of North Atlantic Right Whale Presence To Support Blue Economy Management

entry.content: Effective modeling of endangered marine mammal species, such as the North Atlantic Right Whale, is critical for balancing marine conservation with the growing blue economy. Passive acoustic monitoring data collected by autonomous underwater vehicles provide new opportunities for localized marine species detection and oceanographic sensing, but introduce complex statistical challenges such as zero inflation, imperfect detection, and intricate dependence structures. In response, we propose the Deep Zero-Inflated Bernoulli (DeepZIB) model, a deep statistical method which jointly models latent species presence and conditional detection probabilities while learning complex habitat relationships from heterogeneous covariate information. We establish theoretical results on the model’s structural properties and conduct simulation experiments to demonstrate its ability to recover underlying parameters and latent presence fields. Application to real-world passive acoustic monitoring data on the North Atlantic Right Whale along the U.S. East Coast demonstrates improved model adequacy and predictive performance in capturing the species’ dynamic and spatially varying habitat. We demonstrate DeepZIB’s ability to generate high-resolution, spatially and temporally varying presence maps, providing valuable insights for targeted and risk-aware management of blue economy industries, ranging from offshore and marine energy, to fisheries management and maritime transport

entry.title: Two base rates, two weights: base-rate neglect has a second axis

link.title: Two base rates, two weights: base-rate neglect has a second axis

entry.content: Base-rate neglect is usually treated as one mistake: giving the prior too little weight. Turning co-occurrences into a judgment takes two base-rate corrections, not one: weighting in the prior (how common the outcome is) and dividing out the cue’s own frequency. Under-correcting the prior is classical base-rate neglect. Under-correcting the cue is the cue-density effect, long studied but not usually framed as base-rate neglect’s cue-side analogue. We write both corrections as two weights in one Bayesian equation. The dual-factor heuristic, a leading model of covariation judgment, sits where both equal one-half. Response format fixes which weight a study can measure. A graded rating carries the cue-frequency weight directly. A forced choice between two outcomes cancels it, measuring a separate odds-space weight that agrees with it only at full correction. The cancellation is exact, so same-cue choice proportions carry no information about the cue-frequency weight, not even its direction. A choice between two cues keeps the term, and differing cue frequencies are necessary and sufficient for a softmax choice to depend on it. The same weight appears in six learning-and-memory models (in odds space for signal detection), some exactly, others as a limiting or constructed correspondence. When an experiment keeps only the four cells of a cue x outcome contingency table, each of the six model families projects onto one scalar coordinate, which alone cannot separate the accounts free to sit anywhere along it. On a suitable design the two weights are separately estimable: an experimenter can move either weight’s regressor without moving the other’s. The nested common-weight model excludes a two-coefficient separation by construction. This paper lays out the framework and the rating experiment that tests the separation. A companion paper fits the odds-space cue weight to a colour-flavour dataset.

entry.title: Local conformal prediction for individual causal effects

link.title: Local conformal prediction for individual causal effects

entry.content: Standard CATE estimators become inadequate under strong treatment-effect heterogeneity: confidence intervals for conditional means need not cover individual counterfactual effects. We propose an Individualized Causal Prediction (ICP) framework that constructs finite-sample valid conformal prediction intervals for the individual causal effect of a specific query unit. The method localizes calibration to a causally relevant neighborhood using cosine similarity weighted by Causal Forest variable importance, augments small local samples synthetically, and calibrates intervals with doubly robust AIPW conformity scores satisfying Neyman orthogonality. Under standard identifying assumptions (SUTVA and strong ignorability) and an outcome-independent calibration-set selection condition, the resulting intervals attain marginal coverage at the nominal level. The local design also supports approximately conditional coverage by making calibration scores more representative of the query unit. Experiments on a high-heterogeneity synthetic dataset and the IHDP benchmark demonstrate that local strategies improve point accuracy over global baselines while maintaining nominal or above-nominal coverage.

entry.title: Oracle high-dimensional $M$-estimation using smooth reparameterization for sparsity

link.title: Oracle high-dimensional $M$-estimation using smooth reparameterization for sparsity

entry.content: This paper establishes a unified non-linear regularization framework for high-dimensional $M$-estimation, encompassing both linear regression and Cox’s proportional hazards models. Rather than relying on traditional additive non-convex penalties, the proposed paradigm embeds sparsity directly into the parameter mapping using a smooth ($C^2$) component-wise ReParametrization map for Sparsity (RePS). This geometric formulation dynamically adapts to local parameter scales, successfully suppressing high-dimensional noise and recovering unbiased oracle asymptotic normality under the large-sample limit. Through the Primal-Dual Witness method, we establish a unified oracle equivalence for both model classes under a liberated micro-penalty scaling regime $\lambda \ll n^{-1/2}$, effectively accommodating model-specific structures such as the shift-invariance in survival analysis. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that the RePS framework consistently achieves near-perfect false-positive control and optimal 95\% confidence interval coverage, outperforming conventional non-convex regularizers (SCAD and MCP) which suffer from severe variance inflation and under-coverage due to post-selection noise leakage.

entry.title: Generalized Fiducial Inference for Hybrid Discrete-Continuous Count Data: Theory and Application

link.title: Generalized Fiducial Inference for Hybrid Discrete-Continuous Count Data: Theory and Application

entry.content: High-frequency athlete-tracking data can be summarized as quantile cubes (Thomas and Hannig, 2026): counts of time spent in bins of velocity, acceleration, and movement angle. In our application, each athlete-match session has 100 such bins, with counts ranging from under a hundred to several thousand. Whether a bin’s negative binomial distribution is well approximated by a normal distribution depends on its shape parameter, the product of its mean and dispersion, rather than on the count alone. We develop a hybrid generalized fiducial framework that uses exact negative binomial structural equations where the estimated shape is small and moment-matched normal approximations where it is large. This approach provides uncertainty quantification for hundreds of regression and dispersion parameters without specifying a prior distribution. Only the normal components contribute to the fiducial Jacobian, which has a closed-form block-diagonal structure, and we prove a Bernstein-von Mises theorem for the correctly specified hybrid model. Simulations show near-nominal coverage, agreement with a flat-prior Bayesian analysis, and the importance of partitioning by estimated shape rather than by the mean or observed responses. In 216 sessions from 17 professional women’s soccer athletes, the estimated position effects concentrate at the velocity extremes, while the estimated age effects follow an acceleration gradient. However, an athlete-level permutation check indicates that these patterns are not distinguishable from those obtained under athlete-label permutations.

entry.title: Overlapped We Stand, Separated We Fall: Software Approaches to Diagnosing Separation Phenomena in Categorical Response Models

link.title: Overlapped We Stand, Separated We Fall: Software Approaches to Diagnosing Separation Phenomena in Categorical Response Models

entry.content: In statistical models for categorical responses, including binary, nominal and ordinal responses, a phenomenon called ``separation’’ may occur which can render maximum likelihood estimate nonexistent and/or nonunique. Based on Sablica et al. (2026)’s general characterization of separation phenomena via structure vectors, in this article we discuss computational, numerical and practical aspects of separation phenomena in different software packages, including consequences, remedies and ways of diagnosing them. We further introduce the R package divoRce which provides the most comprehensive software suite to diagnose separation in existence. It allows to check for separation, to distinguish between types of separation, characterize the recession cone and identify variables and observations contributing to separation for almost any categorical response model in the literature, including models with baseline-category link, cumulative link, adjacent-category link and sequential link specifications. Diagnostics are based on methods for computational geometry and linear programming and can be done in floating-point or rational arithmetic with different solvers. The functionality is easily extendible by wrappers and S3 methods to accommodate implementations in third-party packages or of new categorical response models. We discuss our implementation in detail and show our software in action in a wide range of applications. We recommend to incorporate our checks for separation and existence of the MLE as a diagnostic routine in every categorical data analysis both in third-party software implementations and as part of a standard model diagnostic workflow.

entry.title: confoundvis for Visualizing and Reporting Sensitivity to Unmeasured Confounding in R

link.title: confoundvis for Visualizing and Reporting Sensitivity to Unmeasured Confounding in R

entry.content: Sensitivity analysis asks how strong unmeasured confounding would have to be before an observational conclusion changes. Several R packages already calculate established sensitivity quantities, but their outputs use different parameters, objects, and plotting conventions. In this article, we describe confoundvis 0.3.0, an R package designed as a common interface for these analyses. The package stores results from the impact threshold of a confounding variable, the robustness of inference to replacement, partial-R^2 omitted-variable bias analysis, E-values, and Rosenbaum bounds for matched pairs in one confoundsens object. Each result keeps its own parameter and its own published formula. The same functions then draw robustness curves, locate the points at which a conclusion changes, write plain-language reports, and collect several analyses in one table. When a framework describes a confounder by two associations, the package also draws the two-parameter surface on which the familiar single number lies and, where such benchmarks are defined, places measured covariates on the surface. We demonstrate the package with the right heart catheterization data and with a matched-pair study of welders. The native calculations agree with sensemakr, konfound, DOS2, sensitivity2x2xk, and sensitivitymv to numerical or grid precision, and imported EValue results reproduce the reported E-values. The purpose of confoundvis is not to replace the underlying methods or to place their sensitivity parameters on a common scale. Its purpose is to provide a consistent workflow for drawing, comparing, and reporting the results that those methods produce.

entry.title: A parametric mixture cure rate model with competing risks

link.title: A parametric mixture cure rate model with competing risks

entry.content: The well-known standard mixture cure model is widely used to model long-term survivors by distinguishing cured from non-cured individuals in the study population. Since its seminal introduction by Berkson and Gage, numerous extensions have been proposed to enhance its flexibility and applicability across diverse clinical settings. However, most existing extensions focus on a single cause of failure among non-cured individuals, often treating events from alternative causes as censored observations. This limitation may inadequately represent the complexity of survival data in which individuals are exposed to multiple competing causes of failure. In particular, treating competing events as non-informative censoring when estimating the probability of a specific cause of failure may lead to biased estimates of cumulative incidence and potentially misleading clinical interpretations. These limitations motivate the development of flexible survival models that jointly account for long-term survivors and multiple competing causes of failure. In this study, we propose an extension of the standard mixture cure model that incorporates a cure fraction and multiple competing risks within a unified framework. Model parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood using augmented data. The finite-sample performance of the proposed estimators is evaluated through extensive simulation studies, which yield satisfactory results across the scenarios considered. Finally, the proposed methodology is illustrated using melanoma patient data from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database, which include long-term survivors and multiple competing causes of death.

entry.title: Modular Bayesian Inference for Partially Misspecified Mixtures with Uncertain Class Labels

link.title: Modular Bayesian Inference for Partially Misspecified Mixtures with Uncertain Class Labels

entry.content: Scientific inference often involves observations from multiple latent populations whose class memberships are uncertain and must be inferred from available data. While full Bayesian mixture modelling provides a principled approach to joint uncertainty quantification in this setting, often the model is misspecified or less trustworthy for populations that are not the target of the inference, which can distort posterior inference for the parameters of interest. We propose a modular Bayesian framework that safeguards against such biases. We decouple classification from downstream inference using fixed class probabilities, for example from a classifier trained on a subset of labelled data. We then protect inference on the parameters of interest by preventing the likelihood contributions of less trustworthy populations from influencing them. A key benefit of this principled modularization is that it greatly simplifies inference, reducing a fully joint mixture analysis to sampling label allocations, fitting the protected downstream model for each sample, and averaging the resulting posteriors. We establish calibration conditions on these class probabilities under which the proposed procedure preserves the inferential target of the analysis with known labels, and demonstrate the method in synthetic experiments and in cosmological analysis of photometric supernova samples.

link.title: Positive, monotone, and convex Gaussian process regression with Laplacian eigenfunctions

entry.content: We study how to condition an existing Hilbert space Gaussian process (HSGP) expansion on positivity, monotonicity, or convexity throughout an interval. The expansion has Gaussian coefficients whose variances are given by the kernel’s spectral density. At fixed covariance and noise parameters, we retain this coefficient law and represent each complete interval event as a threshold on one coefficient. Integrating out that coefficient gives a strongly log-concave marginal posterior with a normal survival weight, while conditional truncated normal sampling recovers the full constrained law. The construction also covers joint restrictions within the finite expansion. For individual restrictions, we characterize the thresholds through polynomial equations and bound posterior error from conservative numerical evaluation in total variation. Under spectral regularity, the conditioned finite posteriors converge in quadratic Wasserstein distance to the corresponding conditioned underlying GP posteriors as the computational interval expands and higher frequencies are retained. This convergence controls uniform discrepancies in the response and derivatives through the constrained order. Mercury lidar and leaf light-response applications illustrate the consequences for derivative inference.

entry.title: Visualizing Joint Ranking Distributions in Network Meta-Analysis with Hammock Plots

link.title: Visualizing Joint Ranking Distributions in Network Meta-Analysis with Hammock Plots

entry.content: Treatment ranking provides a summary of the relative effectiveness of competing treatments and is a key output of network meta-analysis (NMA). Existing visualizations primarily summarize marginal ranking distributions or present individual treatment hierarchies with limited insight into uncertainty in the overall hierarchy. We introduce hammock plots as a visualization framework for the joint posterior distribution of treatment rankings. Although motivated by treatment ranking in NMA, the proposed framework is broadly applicable to any setting in which uncertainty in posterior rankings is of interest. Specifically, we develop separate hammock plots to display relationships between (a) adjacent treatments or (b) adjacent ranks. Using highlighting, we show how to assess posterior support for selected treatment hierarchies, to evaluate hierarchies identified by ranking metrics against the posterior distribution, and to examine uncertainty within selected regions of the treatment hierarchy. We apply the proposed visualizations to a thrombolytic treatment network, which revealed patterns in the posterior ranking distribution and the location of uncertainty in treatment hierarchies that were difficult to identify using existing ranking graphics. link.title: Inference for Directions in Canonical Correlation Analysis with Partially Paired Data

entry.content: Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) is a classical tool for learning linear associations between two data views, and inference on canonical directions is the key for interpreting their coefficients and detecting interesting relationships. The key challenge is to incorporate the additional marginal information while accounting for its dependence on the paired sample used to estimate the canonical directions. To address this issue, we propose coupled augmentation functions that jointly use the marginal information from both views and construct a one-step estimator based on the resulting corrections. This result provides a sign-invariant Wald test statistic for detecting important variables in canonical directions. entry.title: A plug-in estimator of the non-iterative conditional expectation g-formula using long short-term memory models

link.title: A plug-in estimator of the non-iterative conditional expectation g-formula using long short-term memory models

entry.content: The non-iterative conditional expectation (NICE) plug-in estimator of the g-formula can be used to estimate the causal effects of sustained treatment strategies, even in the presence of treatment-confounder feedback, under the assumptions of exchangeability, positivity, and consistency. In practical applications, parametric models are commonly used to estimate the joint distribution of confounders, treatments, and outcomes over time. As an alternative to parametric models, long short-term memory (LSTM) models, designed to capture both short-term patterns and long-range dependencies in sequential data, may better accommodate complex temporal dependencies among time-varying confounders, treatments, and outcomes. However, the validity of statistical inferences of a plug-in estimator based on LSTM models has not yet been investigated. Here, we provide proof of principle that, under a complex data generation mechanism that resembles data from a cohort of persons with HIV and sufficiently large sample sizes, an LSTM-based NICE g-formula plug-in estimator results in less bias than parametric estimators while achieving near-nominal coverage for 95\% confidence intervals. This work is intended to spur the development of a theoretical framework that encompasses deep learning plug-in estimators for causal inference based on high-dimensional longitudinal data.

link.title: Doubly Robust Estimation and Inference for Longitudinal Win Probabilities with Ordinal Outcomes in Observational Studies

entry.content: Repeated ordinal outcomes capture how treatment benefits and harms evolve over time. We develop doubly robust estimation and inference for visit-specific win probabilities and their prespecified weighted summaries, with Desirability of Outcome Ranking as a motivating example. Baseline confounding is addressed through augmented inverse-probability weighting (AIPW) of treatment-specific marginal category probabilities or joint multinomial targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE). We consider fold-specific and pooled targeting and establish conditions for double-robust consistency and semiparametric efficiency under participant-level cross-fitting. When only one nuisance model is correctly specified, inference based only on the efficient influence function may be invalid. For smooth parametric nuisance models, we derive covariance corrections from the complete estimating procedure, including targeting. When a correctly specified propensity model is estimated by maximum likelihood, a simplified score correction accommodates convergent flexible outcome learners without requiring their derivatives. The corrected covariance estimators retain within-participant dependence and support visit-specific, weighted-summary, and joint inference across repeated assessments. Simulations supported double robustness, demonstrated the importance of cross-fitting with overfit learners, and showed improved marginal and joint confidence coverage with the proposed corrections. TMLE, particularly with pooled targeting, often had lower root mean squared error under adequate treatment overlap, whereas AIPW was more stable under weak overlap. An electronic health record study of hospitalized adults with an acute respiratory illness illustrates how the trajectory and weighted summary reveal complementary aspects of the treatment comparison.

entry.title: A copula-based competing risks model with application to cancer risk estimation in family studies

link.title: A copula-based competing risks model with application to cancer risk estimation in family studies

entry.content: Cancer risk estimation tools are used by clinicians to evaluate the risk of individuals who carry high-risk pathogenic variants. In this article, we propose a new competing risks model designed to provide personalized estimates of the risk of developing breast or ovarian cancer as the first event among women carrying pathogenic variants in the BRCA1 gene. Our approach incorporates both the personal and complete family history of cancer of these high-risk women and introduces some flexibly in the modeling of the dependence among members of the same family. We use a Gaussian copula with a correlation matrix expressed in terms of the kinship coefficients of pairs of members. Furthermore, we develop an iterative estimation algorithm to estimate the parameters of the underlying model in the presence of a selection bias inherent to the family recruitment process. The performance of the proposed method is evaluated through a simulation study. An application to the Breast Cancer Family Registry data highlights the ability of the model to provide personalized estimation of the risk of developing breast cancer or ovarian cancer as the first event within the competing risks framework.

entry.title: Choose your own adventure: How data source selection shapes urban accessibility analyses

link.title: Choose your own adventure: How data source selection shapes urban accessibility analyses

entry.content: Urban park accessibility shapes mental health, physical well-being, and community cohesion. Measuring it is thus central to urban and landscape planning. Although researchers have debated the impacts of different accessibility measures on analysis results, scant attention has been paid to variability from data source selection. Do the results of accessibility analyses vary depending on the dataset used to define park locations and attributes? We compare four widely used geospatial data sources - OpenStreetMap, Esri, SafeGraph, and The Trust for Public Land - by validating their data and measuring park access across two cities. These datasets purport to cover the same spatial features, but our findings reveal wide discrepancies in accessibility results, driven by differences in dataset completeness, coverage, and accuracy between the sources. We provide guidelines for selecting and carefully validating data for accessibility analyses, as these decisions directly impact the accuracy and equity of downstream urban park planning and decision-making.

entry.title: Structural equation modelling–based meta-analytic model for diagnostic test accuracy studies

link.title: Structural equation modelling–based meta-analytic model for diagnostic test accuracy studies

entry.content: Bivariate random-effects models are commonly used to jointly synthesize sensitivity and specificity in diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) meta-analysis. However, existing approaches may be sensitive to distributional assumptions and may produce biased estimates of accuracy and between-study heterogeneity with sparse meta-analytic data. We conducted extensive simulations under varying study, sample-size, accuracy, and heterogeneity conditions. We assessed model performance using bias, root mean squared error (RMSE), confidence interval width, empirical 95% coverage probability (CP), and convergence. We generated study-specific random effects from bivariate normal, t, and Laplace distributions to assess robustness to distributional misspecification. We also applied the models to two empirical DTA datasets. The BSEM generally produced smaller bias and RMSE and nominal-level CP for pooled sensitivity and specificity than the BLMM, while the BGLMM generally yielded results between the two approaches. The BLMM showed stable convergence but tended to underestimate between-study heterogeneity. We observed similar performance patterns under the three random-effects distributions. In the empirical applications, differences between model estimates were generally consistent with patterns observed in the simulations. Overall, the proposed BSEM provided a flexible alternative approach for jointly modelling sensitivity and specificity in DTA meta-analysis, with performance that was generally favourable relative to the BLMM and comparable to the BGLMM across the simulated and empirical settings considered.

link.title: Mixture of Censored Partially Linear Experts Models for Symmetric or Asymmetric Data with or without Outlying Observations: A novel approach with two-piece scale-mixture of normal distributions

entry.content: Finite mixture of partially linear model and finite mixture of experts models offer flexible tools for analyzing heterogeneous data, especially when covariates influence subgroup structure. Partially linear models further enhance this flexibility by combining linear and nonlinear effects. In many applications, however, censoring and departures from normality complicate estimation. To address these issues, we introduce a semiparametric mixture of censored partially linear expert models based on the two-piece scale mixture of normal family, which can accommodate skewness, heavy tails, and censoring. The proposed framework enables closed-form expressions in the E-step of an ECME algorithm, avoiding MCMC-based approximations and yielding stable maximum likelihood estimates. Simulation studies and real data analyses demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in settings with both heterogeneity and censoring.

entry.title: A Bayesian machine learning approach to direct and spillover effects in cluster-randomized trials with noncompliance

link.title: A Bayesian machine learning approach to direct and spillover effects in cluster-randomized trials with noncompliance

entry.content: We develop a Bayesian machine learning approach for estimating direct and spillover effects in cluster-randomized trials with treatment noncompliance. To flexibly model outcomes and treatment receipt while accounting for within-cluster dependence, we combine Bayesian additive regression trees with cluster-level random effects. We augment the outcome regression with a peer-treatment clever covariate, defined as the predicted mean proportion of treated peers from a preliminary receipt model, to mitigate regularization-induced distortion of the effect decomposition. Within a Bayesian g-computation framework, we estimate cluster-average intent-to-treat effects and cluster-average local average treatment effects and examine sensitivity to the cross-world restrictions underlying their decomposition. Simulation studies show reduced bias under model misspecification, while the correctly specified parametric models show expected frequentist properties. We find that the clever covariate improves the decomposition of the total effect into direct and spillover components under moderate or strong spillover, with similar gains in smaller clusters. Its benefits vary with spillover strength, and the $95\%$ credible intervals remain conservative. An application to the Primary School Deworming Project in Kenya suggests reduced infection risk, with a larger estimated contribution from individual treatment receipt than from peer receipt. Overall, our approach provides a flexible Bayesian estimation of direct and spillover effect decomposition in the presence of treatment noncompliance.

link.title: Beyond exponential tilting: sharp asymptotics and improved importance sampling for rare events

entry.content: A classical approach for importance sampling (IS) of a rare event is to tilt the measure using its large deviation minimizer, thereby shifting the proposal mean towards the event set. While this tilt is log-efficient, we show that the coefficient of variation of the resulting estimator still grows like $\varepsilon^{-1/4}$ in the small-noise limit $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Motivated by sharp large deviation asymptotics and the local geometry of the event set at the minimizer, we propose improvements using a control variate or an anisotropic, non-Gaussian proposal. We prove, up to truncations that hold with high probability, and confirm empirically in high-dimensional examples, that the former bounds the coefficient of variation and the latter makes it vanish, so that a bounded number of samples suffices. Our analysis addresses both the coefficient of variation of the different proposals and their necessary and sufficient sample size based on the Kullback–Leibler divergence of the IS target from the proposal; both yield the same rates in $\varepsilon$. We demonstrate the resulting samplers, including a variant that blends the classical and the new proposal across noise levels, for a stochastic Korteweg–de Vries equation with thousands of random inputs.

entry.title: Geometry-informed importance sampling for rare events

link.title: Geometry-informed importance sampling for rare events

entry.content: We propose GeoIS, a new importance sampling method for estimating rare event probabilities for an underlying Gaussian distribution that exploits asymptotic theory and local event geometry. The proposal distribution is a mixture of two components. The first component draws a Gaussian along the boundary near the instanton and adds to it an exponentially distributed shift into the rare event. This component is derived from the known asymptotic approximation to the optimal zero-variance proposal distribution. The second mixture component is designed to cover missing event mass due to boundary-approximation mismatch, thereby preserving unbiasedness. We rigorously analyze this sampling strategy’s performance as a function of event geometry, dimension, rarity level, and number $N$ of importance samples. Under explicit and relatively mild conditions on the former three features, we prove that the squared relative error of GeoIS is bounded by $c/N$ with high probability, for an absolute constant $c$. We implement our method numerically in several examples, including a diffusion PDE problem. The numerical experiments exhibit the qualitative dependence on geometry, dimension, rarity and sample size predicted by the theory, and show that GeoIS markedly outperforms importance sampling methods that use a fully Gaussian proposal distribution.

entry.title: Beyond Scalar Leaderboards: Adaptive Sampling for Pareto Frontier Identification in Multi-Objective LLM Arenas

link.title: Beyond Scalar Leaderboards: Adaptive Sampling for Pareto Frontier Identification in Multi-Objective LLM Arenas

entry.content: The evaluation of large language models (LLMs) is inherently multi-objective, as different models may offer different tradeoffs across performance dimensions such as math, code, and writing. Because such evaluations are often based on costly and time-consuming human feedback, it is important to draw reliable conclusions using as few comparisons as possible. In this paper, we present Vector-Borda Empirical-Gap Elimination (VB-EGE), a fixed-confidence adaptive sampling algorithm for efficiently identifying models on the Pareto frontier in arena-style evaluation, where each comparison evaluates a pair of models on a prompt with respect to a selected performance dimension. VB-EGE progressively eliminates models from an active set once sufficient statistical evidence has been accumulated to certify their Pareto status. Under a multi-objective Bradley-Terry model, we show that VB-EGE returns the correct Pareto frontier with high probability and derive an instance-dependent upper bound on its sample complexity. We further establish a worst-case lower bound showing that VB-EGE is minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors. Simulations and experiments on three real-world Arena datasets (Arena, SearchArena, and VisionArena) demonstrate VB-EGE’s empirical effectiveness.

entry.title: Strong Simultaneous Inference for Restricted Mean Survival Time Processes in Multi-Arm Trials under Covariate-Adaptive Randomization

link.title: Strong Simultaneous Inference for Restricted Mean Survival Time Processes in Multi-Arm Trials under Covariate-Adaptive Randomization

entry.content: Confirmatory trials increasingly test several treatments against a common control, and many balance prognostic factors through covariate-adaptive randomization (CAR). For time-to-event endpoints, they usually rely on the stratified log-rank test and the hazard ratio, but the former may lose power and the latter its clear interpretation when hazards are not proportional. The restricted mean survival time (RMST) provides an interpretable alternative, yet inference for multiple RMST comparisons under CAR remains largely unexplored. We first derive the joint asymptotic distribution of the standard Kaplan–Meier RMST estimators in multi-arm trials. Under Pocock–Simon minimization, their limiting covariance contains a design term that arises only when the randomization factors interact in their effect on survival. A stratum-standardized estimator removes this term and remains valid when censoring depends on the strata. We then develop test statistics that account for the shared control and the randomization design. Calibrated by a Gaussian multiplier, the resulting max-$T$ procedures control the family-wise error rate and give simultaneous confidence bands over restriction times. In simulations, the method controls the Type I error rate under various randomization procedures and outperforms the stratified log-rank test when the benefit wanes. An application based on the three-arm ICON6 trial illustrates its practicality.

link.title: On the Accuracy of Approximate Leave-One-Out with Blockwise Nonsmooth Regularization in High-dimensions

entry.content: Approximate leave-one-out (ALO) refers to methods that provide computationally efficient and statistically accurate approximations to leave-one-out risk estimation. These methods have recently attracted increased attention because of their connections to other important problems, including machine unlearning and data valuation. For empirical risk minimization, ALO methods often rely on a few Newton steps and therefore require smooth loss functions and regularizers. In high-dimensional problems, however, regularizers are frequently non-smooth. This has motivated the development of heuristic ALO methods for non-smooth regularization, whose empirical accuracy is often strong but whose theoretical justification remains limited. In this paper, we study the accuracy of a heuristic ALO method for a broad class of non-differentiable penalties that promote block sparsity in the proportional high-dimensional regime. entry.title: Active Pilot Sampling for Multi-fidelity Estimation in Stochastic Optimization

link.title: Active Pilot Sampling for Multi-fidelity Estimation in Stochastic Optimization

entry.content: Stochastic optimization with high-fidelity nonlinear models is often computationally prohibitive because each objective evaluation requires sampling-based uncertainty quantification inside an outer optimization loop. Multi-fidelity estimators, such as approximate control variates (ACV), can reduce this cost by exploiting cheaper low-fidelity models, but they require model-output covariance information to determine control-variate weights and sample allocations. These covariances are generally unknown and must be estimated through pilot sampling. Existing pilot-sampling strategies primarily address one-off estimation and do not exploit the structure of iterative stochastic optimization, where covariance information may vary smoothly across the design domain and can be shared across optimization queries. We propose an active pilot-sampling framework that learns a probabilistic emulator of the model-output covariance matrix using a positive-definite parameterization based on matrix-logarithm-transformed correlations and log standard deviations. The emulator provides design-specific covariance estimates for constructing ACV estimators at new optimization queries, avoiding repeated independent covariance estimation at every design. Active-learning acquisition functions allocate pilot samples to designs where covariance information is most uncertain and most relevant to the outer optimization objective. We demonstrate the method on a four-branch benchmark and a multi-fidelity Bayesian optimal experimental design application for sensor placement and measurement-time selection in a convection-diffusion system. The results show improved optimization performance relative to single-fidelity Monte Carlo and simpler pilot-sampling strategies.

entry.title: Bayesian Neural Networks via Dirichlet Process Priors on the Data-Generating Distribution for Randomized Value Functions in Deep Reinforcement Learning

link.title: Bayesian Neural Networks via Dirichlet Process Priors on the Data-Generating Distribution for Randomized Value Functions in Deep Reinforcement Learning

entry.content: Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) offer a principled framework for quantifying epistemic uncertainty. However, standard weight-space priors yield complex, high-dimensional neural network posteriors that are computationally prohibitive to sample from, and popular approximate inference schemes often fail to capture epistemic uncertainty effectively—a failure mode particularly acute in reinforcement learning (RL) \citep{osband2018randomized}. To resolve this challenge, we introduce a new class of BNNs that quantify uncertainty by placing Bayesian nonparametric Dirichlet Process (DP) priors directly on the underlying data-generating distribution rather than on network parameters. Building on this foundation, we develop DP-DQN, a reinforcement learning algorithm that leverages DP-BNNs to maintain posterior distributions over value functions and perform efficient Thompson sampling. By grounding randomized value functions in Bayesian nonparametrics, DP-DQN unifies data-driven posterior reweighting (via the Bayesian Bootstrap) with generative prior hypotheses injected directly through the DP base measure, enabling decisive ``deep exploration’’ with a single neural network without the overhead of multi-network ensembles.

entry.title: Functional meta-analysis of survival curves across reporting formats and time points

link.title: Functional meta-analysis of survival curves across reporting formats and time points

entry.content: Meta-analyses of survival outcomes commonly pool log hazard ratios or survival probabilities at selected time points. When reporting formats and observation times differ across studies, methods are needed to use available survival information for estimation at a common target time. We propose a functional random-effects model on the complementary log–log scale that synthesizes Kaplan–Meier curves and survival probabilities at discrete times as functional data. Studies that do not report survival at the target time contribute to its estimation through the use of their observed curves to estimate group-specific mean functions. The estimated between-group contrast is interpreted as a log hazard ratio under proportional hazards and as a time-specific log cumulative hazard ratio under non-proportional hazards. In simulations with delayed effects and crossing survival curves, the root mean squared error for the log cumulative hazard ratio was lower than that of the two-stage Cox method, and interval coverage was close to the nominal level. In an application to disease-free survival in resectable non-small cell lung cancer, the two-stage Cox method estimated an average hazard ratio, whereas the proposed method captured nonlinear changes in the cumulative hazard ratio over time.
